 researchers derived an order-by-order approximation scheme similar to Janssen's
scheme within renormalization group theory, and similar to similar calculations
in the past, this approach replicated previously found critical properties of
the system, and yielded a critical exponent list that matches a 2D Ising
lattice's behavior, exactly.

This study aims to explain in detail zeroing neural networks, particularly in regards to solving time-dependent matrix problems that involve predicting future states from past observations. Key focuses include deriving mathematical formulas for functions that involve exponential decay and recovery, account for initial conditions and inputs over time, and how specific neural network architectures can be designed to represent these functions. Additionally, this paper discusses how to train such models to accurately predict outcomes, given limited data. Relevant theoretical frameworks and code implementations are also reviewed and an example code snippet provided for better understanding.

The overall processing mechanism in biological retinas consists of summing local cell responses in a specific pattern of on and off pathways. Building on this concept, researchers have introduced a simple retinal model comprising on-off centers and surrounds. However, it is not capable of replicating the complexity of biological responses, and as such, has primarily been used as a basic preprocessing step. In this study, it is demonstrated that this model can serve as an efficient and robust feature extractor by utilising a network called ResNet50, trained on the CIFAR10 dataset. When employed as a preceeding layer to ResNet50, the new structure referred to as COS-Net achieves significantly higher accuracy and enhanced level of robustness when faced with challenges such as data augmentation, noise, and adversarial attacks. Moreover, the results of the exposition are also tested on the CIFAR100 dataset, resulting in a substantial gain in accuracy when compared to the original model. In accordance with the standards set by the community, all the associated code will be shared post this study.

In wide-field X-ray astronomy, deep observations over large areas and sensitive detection of faint sources make the acquisition rate a critical factor. Achieving this requires an efficient use of telescope focal plane coverage and optimized data reduction techniques. The analytical methods previously employed for the BeppoSAX nitrogen charged-coupled device (CCD) camera have several limitations including spatial and energy non-uniformity, high background levels, and geometric distortions. The evaluation of a modified analysis method aimed at enhancing wide-field coverage and focal plane accessibility revealed significant benefits for large area observations. The refined methodology yields uniform and high-quality images with minimal geometric distortions, demonstrating potential advantages in wide-field X-ray observations.

The core of topological band theory, Bloch's theorem, is a fundamental concept that has been applied to study insulating systems with periodic magnetic arrangements. However, it encounters difficulties in materials with complex, non-Abelian flux configurations, such as those caused by charge density waves. Our research finds that the magnetic version of Bloch's theorem remains valid in twisted bilayer graphene under a $2\pi$ flux brought about by charge density waves, resulting in a consistent Chern number. Moreover, we discover a reentrant flat band at half-filling that arises from the intersection of Landau levels with the Brillouin zone edges due to the effects of twist and flux.

Inspired by a desire to protect user privacy, we propose an innovative form of textsteeganography. Our method leverages an LSTM model to automatically generate fake text that can be used to conceal secret messages. Initially, we trained an LSTM to create normal text and a specific type of text based on a given password. Subsequently, we modified the model to hide secret messages in normal text. While our results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, the quality of the generated text is not yet satisfactory for practical use, so we are actively seeking ways to enhance our method's effectiveness.

In power system optimization, the unit commitment (UC) constraint examination is a critical operation that needs to be performed multiple times during optimization. For large-scale UC problems, determining whether a proposed solution violates any constraint can be very time-consuming and often causes issues with fast UC solutions. In this paper, we introduce a machine learning-based approach to significantly speed up UC constraint examination by learning and utilizing cost models. We leverage neural networks to approximate UC problems and develop a fast evaluation method for UC constraints using a constraint approximation table. Moreover, we propose a technique to rapidly check whether a proposed UC solution violates generator and boiler constraints. The simulation results on the IEEE 300-bus and IEEE 914-bus systems reveal that our proposed method outperforms current techniques with a substantial reduction of up to 90% in UC constraint examination time. The fast UC solutions and efficient economic outcomes validate the applicability of these fast constraints to fast UC algorithms.

Measurements using nuclear magnetic resonance and heat capacity techniques were conducted on samples of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ under pressure, showing how pressure affects its magnetic phase transition. At room temperature and pressures below 1 GPa, the sample exhibits two phases, Heisenberg and spin liquid. As pressure increases past 1 GPa, the Heisenberg phase transitions into an intermediate phase with Ir$^{4+}$ ions that order magnetically and then into a higher pressure phase with ions that do not order. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectra and heat capacity plots reveal how this transition affects the sample's magnetic entropy. Ir ion magnetism is found to be highly correlated with their structural changes, with the transition into the high-pressure phase occurring at 9 GPa and 290 K. Heat capacity plots indicate that the sample's magnetic and structural transitions become more complex at higher pressures, with the sample's enthalpy of transition increasing.

This research develops a theoretical foundation for nonparametric synthetic control methods by establishing a comprehensive framework for synthetic counterfactual series based on nearby causal influence. Within this context, the synthetic counterfactual series is derived from a function F that is determined by treatment effects, unaffected by confounding variables, and meets specific conditions. The study identifies necessary conditions for accurate root-n identification of treatment effects and presents two key methods for making inference at optimal efficiency levels. Initially, a t-statistic is employed for inference, but it's shown to be less efficient when the process involves discrete changes. An alternative method using Bayesian inference is introduced, yielding enhanced efficiency for such cases. A simulation study compares inference types and concludes with an analysis of the synthetic control's application in valuing the impact of Social Security.

Recent advancements in graph learning technologies have led to increased discussion about the protection of private and sensitive data. The Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy provides a metric that quantifies the similarity of graph structures without disclosing node identity. Nevertheless, calculating this discrepancy from distributed, high-dimensional graph data while preserving data confidentiality remains a challenging task. To address this issue, this paper presents a metric computation method that leverages the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy and ensures the confidentiality of the source graphs through the application of differential privacy. To achieve this, a theoretical connection is first established between the Gromov-Wasserweight distance and the synthetic graph generated using the Q-mle algorithm. Next, an optimization algorithm is developed to estimate the synthetic graph of the target node through query responses from the source nodes, utilizing the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy as the objective function. The method ensures that the query responses conform to differential privacy standards, thereby preserving the confidentiality of the source graphs. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method accurately calculates the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy while maintaining data confidentiality and showing a positive relationship with the sample size.

Recent experiments have demonstrated the capability of extremely intense, ultrashort laser pulses to generate electron jets that can be polarized at distances far beyond the laser's propagation distance. This phenomenon occurs due to the laser pulse's self-focusing, which happens at the plasma density gradient where it experiences a complex combination of spatial and temporal plasma density modifications. This process results in a further increase in the laser's intensity, leading to the creation of a highly collimated and extremely intense electron beam that can be polarized. This article describes the development of a simplified model that explains the mechanism of electron beam formation, which agrees with experimental results including the observation of electron beams traveling at super-Lundmark angles. The model also predicts a direct proportionality between the laser's normalized transverse electric field and the polarization angle of the electron beam, which it predicts to be $\theta_p \propto a_n^2$. Although the model presented has its limitations, it offers a simplified and clear explanation of the mechanism producing the electron beam, which has been modeled in the past using full Vlasov-Maxwell equations.

A detailed study of the radioactive decay of $^{190}$Pt and its companions has been conducted at Canada's SNOLAB facility under extremely low background conditions. For the first time, researchers observed the $2
u$ decay of $^{190}$Pt and other neighboring isotopes. Combining this observation with large datasets collected over three years, precise bounds were established at 90% confidence for the half-lives of $0
u 2 eta$, $2
u$, and $0
u eta eta$ decay in several platinum isotopes. Furthermore, as a byproduct of the experiment, researchers set new limits on dark matter and nuclear processes such as spin-independent and spin-dependent dark matter interactions and axion-induced processes within platinum.

The calculation of the renormalization group evolution of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge is crucial for understanding QCD anomalies and possible quark-gluon plasma formation. This system's behavior is governed by a key relation tying the charges of the axial-vector, vector, and scalar types. A novel approach using dimensional regularization is capable of accurately calculating all standard model charges, including their relationships and anomalies. This is achieved through a straightforward method of introducing the Dirac delta function and the principal value of the 1/d space integral. As a result, the calculation of the axial-vector charge anomaly in conjunction with tree-level gauge coupling is straightforward and matches established results.

A crucial step in creating realistic avatar characters is generating a skin tone.  Achieving a uniform tone across multiple close-circuit cameras is essential for creating a cohesive visual experience.  We developed a novel method to produce a natural and consistent skin appearance by analyzing data from cameras positioned at different angles.  Our system employs a dynamic skin model that adapts to changing lighting conditions in real-time, allowing for accurate color reproduction across cameras.  The output of our system is characterized by a distinct specular shine and smooth undertone distribution, resulting in a remarkably lifelike skin appearance.  Preliminary evaluations through user studies have confirmed the effectiveness of our method in creating a natural appearance, with scores comparable to actual human skin tone.

The extended version of the Ermakov system, known as the coupled Ermakov system, is explored in n dimensions.  This system has been shown to have several key characteristics.  First, its own symmetries exist independently.  Next, a set of conservation laws corresponds exactly to the symmetries present within the system.  Finally, the coupled Ermakov system itself can be viewed as a combination of two independent equations that each possess a symmetry and a corresponding conservation law.  One of these equations is non-Lagrangian.

The Transit Feed Specification (TFS) provides standardized data from public transportation sources, enabling the download of schedules and routes using easy-to-parse APIs. Approximately 20% of serving agencies face difficulties generating this data, often due to outdated or non-functional APIs. To overcome this, a new method utilizing a two-part Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is introduced, in conjunction with the existing GTFS-Scanner, to extract desired Feed Information. The proposed architecture is demonstrated with a successful implementation in San Francisco, and this method is expected to be adapted for other cities.

Prototype-based few-shot learning models like Prototypical Network learn from 
class prototypes obtained from updated mean andificioners after collecting 
support samples. Yet, when there's a shortage of support data, these 
prototypes lack to convey the characteristics of the classes they represent. 
To overcome this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach where 
prototypes are replaced with 'class-type prototypes', containing a class 
feature-vector, a sample-feature-matrix, and a label vector. We use this 
class-type prototype to develop a unified framework for classification, 
where the objective is to minimize the Euclidean distance between the test 
sample and the class-type prototype. Since the class-type prototype's 
feature-matrix dimension matches the test sample's dimensionality, it can 
be learned directly from the training data, allowing the class-type 
prototypes to capture the class's characteristics accurately. As a result, 
this approach outperforms existing methods in few-shot learning scenarios, 
partially because the class-type prototypes can convey the class's 
features more effectively than traditional prototypes. When tested on 
datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and mini-ImageNet, this approach 
consistently delivers a higher classification accuracy than Prototypical 
Networks.

We are analyzing non-invertible symmetries that can be applied consistently in gapped systems, such as those in higher-dimensional topological phases, where the universal properties are characterized as anomalies. A notable aspect is that symmetries with no invertibility and anomalies can be found in both local and non-local situations. Here, we discuss a general theorem (Goldstone's theorem for non-invertible symmetries) that explores the implications of inverting the non-invertible symmetries on the boundary of gapped systems. The theorem reveals that inverting the non-invertible symmetry on the boundary leads to a non-trivial symplectic transformation of the anomaly equation $\mathcal{J}\cdot\partial X=\lambda X$. We observe that the phase of the wavefunction has a geometric constraint similar to the $\mathcal{U}(1)$ phase, determining the form of the anomaly equation, and a linear equation describing the flow of $\partial X$. The solution of the anomaly equation defines the form of the phase. This theorem has significant implications for inverting the non-invertible symmetry on the boundary of topological phases, such as those of fractional topological insulators and non-invertible topological interfaces.

A semi-transitive graph has no directed paths between neighbours of neighbours, 
split graphs are defined as the difference of two cliques, we investigate split 
graphs that are semi-transitive or have non-crossing cliques and find bounds 
on their density and a characterisation based on even and odd holes.

A cutting-edge approach has been developed to pinpoint events featuring the decay of a tau particle into hadrons, by utilizing the San Francisco algorithm in conjunction with a deep neural network. This innovative method employs the deep neural network to distinguish between tau decays and those of muons and electrons, whereas the San Francisco algorithm identifies tau particle signatures within hadronic decays. Both the deep neural network and the San Francisco algorithm were trained using simulated data containing real data events as references. Validation was performed using a range of data samples, including tau particle decays, background signals from muons and electrons, and events lacking a signature tau particle. Observations indicated a high level of correlation between the deep neural network's performance and experimental data expectations, with results as follows: For events containing the decay of a tau particle into three particles, the efficiency was approximately 59.9%, across all phases of state and unit conditions; those not featuring the decay of a tau particle showed minimal false positives of less than one in a thousand; Efficiency and accuracy varied between $58-65$ % for events containing the decay of a tau particle into one, three, or seven particles, across all phases of state and unit conditions.

Future sky surveys, notably LSST and Euclid, will experience high levels of data corruption and noise, necessitating advanced analysis techniques to accurately classify their findings and estimate their parameters. Traditional methods, such as maximum likelihood, may not always yield the most efficient results, particularly when dealing with imperfect data. A study evaluates and compares the effectiveness of traditional maximum likelihood and contemporary Bayesian neural networks on simulated supernova data. The sample analysis shows that Bayesian neural networks consistently outperform maximum likelihood on this data set, with one variant offering sub-second analysis times capable of handling up to 100 million data points.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within photonic lattice fibers, featuring fluorine-vapor-filled microcores. Through experimental measurements and theoretical simulations, the thermal noise levels associated with these modal interactions are quantified and attributed to fundamental and next-nearest longitudinal modes. Notably, the peak strain associated with these strains corresponds to a mechanical energy loss per unit length of around 10^-3 ln^2(km/s^2) at 7 MHz. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the ability to remotely monitor a fiber tensometer with nanometer resolution using phase matching techniques.

The foundation theorem, originally applied by Brink and Humphreys in studying coinvariants of Lie algebras, has been extended here to cover the case for B-type Coxeter groups. This extended theorem will serve as a foundational approach for the analysis of homologies of the balanced spherical product of the permutation representation and the positive root representation within the setting of constant term subalgebras. As a result, we arrive at an algorithmic means for calculating the balanced homology groups throughout theainfold of the balanced spherical product of the permutation representation and the positive root representation within the setting of constant term subalgebras.

Two related variations of the knapsack problem, known as the Set-Union Knapsack Problem (UKP) and Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP), are used in diverse applications ranging from data mining to combinatorial game theory. In the UKP, the objective is to achieve the highest possible set-union cost while staying within a budget, whereas BMCP involves covering the maximum number of items at or below a specified budget. A novel solution approach has been developed that combines these two problems into one and employs a local search method utilizing a fast and efficient evaluation function, thus yielding highly competitive results for both the UKP and BMCP. This strategy has produced numerous new UKP and BMCP instance best-solutions, surpassing existing records. A thorough comparison with previous state-of-the-art algorithms, including those specifically tailored for BMCP, was conducted, demonstrating the innovative solution's exceptional performance across a wide range of problem instances.

In the complex field of online gambling, understanding and predicting player churn presents a significant challenge. This issue is crucial, however, as retaining existing customers often proves to be less costly and less competitive than acquiring new ones. In our analysis, we evaluated churn prediction in online gambling from two distinct perspectives: the individual player and the company. By examining data from a major online casino operator, we investigated factors contributing to player churn and the effectiveness of machine learning models in predicting it. The results revealed that specific machine learning methods, such as Random Forest and XGBoost, offer superior performance in this context, achieving high accuracy rates and statistical significance. The outcome of this study can serve as a basis for future optimization strategies in online gambling, enabling companies to refine their services and tailor their policies to meet the needs of their players, ultimately retaining valuable customers.

We examine the Ising Field Theory, particularly its behavior in the Ising Universality Class, focusing on the Yang-Lee critical point and the associated critical exponent $\rho$. Utilizing an IR-safe expansion around the YLC, we calculate the exponent $\rho$ in high orders to establish its value. The resulting estimate for $\rho$ aligns well with numerical simulations results from the lattice model. Additionally, we use the IR-safe expansion to determine the value of the Yang-Lee edge singularities in the complex $m$ plane. The location of these singularities is accurately represented in the subcritical regime. The findings suggest that the YLC's behavior is accurately captured through an IR-safe expansion around this point. The method also allows for a unified description of the properties across both 2D and 4D Ising Universality Class systems. The approach can be extended to other critical points within the Ising Universality Class. The same method can be applied to other critical points within the Ising Universality Class. The approach can also be applied to other critical points within the Ising Universality Class. The approach has the potential to study critical points in both 2D and 4D systems. The approach has the potential to study critical points in both 2D and 4D systems.

The large-momentum behavior of gluon Transverse-Momentum-Dependent Distributions (tMDs) is investigated using a framework known as Large-Momentum Behavior Beyond Perturbation Theory (LMBLPT). This approach is grounded in the Mellin transformation of LMBLPT's resummation formula and provides a non-perturbative framework for analyzing LMBLPT results. The paper demonstrates that the gluon tMD retains a significant power-like term at large transverse-momentum, which scales with $p_T^4$. Notably, this power-like term is linked to the gluon distribution function $g_{1}$, which suggests a crucial role for gluons in shaping the transverse-momentum spectrum of hard processes. The study also outlines a strategy for extracting the gluon distribution's higher moments from precise measurements of $Z$ boson $p_T$ spectra at the Future Circular Collider (FCC).

In the photon-photon interaction that occurs in ultra-peripheral collisions of heavy ions, the emergence of low-momentum electron-positron pairs at mid-rapidity is a potential sign of phenomena such as photonuclear reactions and the interaction of electrons and positrons with nuclei. The creation of these leptons in the electromagnetic field of heavy ions is analyzed numerically, taking into account the photon field of a spherical nucleus. The characteristics of the production of leptons in the electromagnetic field of separate nuclei, ranging from 39 to 258, are calculated at the energies of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), and are then compared to simulations that include the full time-dependent photon field. The influence of a strong magnetic field on the leptons during nuclear collisions is also a significant aspect of these processes.

To minimize the number of bicycle-related injuries, an advanced safety system is developed to offer real-time advice to bicyclists. The system, known as RIDE, utilizes a camera-based approach to identify potential hazards and offer personalized guidance based on the cyclist's experience level and the level of risk. By employing a wearable head-mounted camera, RIDE captures the surrounding environment and uses computer vision algorithms to detect and classify various road dangers such as vehicles, pedestrian footsteps, and road obstructions. The effectiveness of the proposed system is evaluated through a study involving 1,501 images of risk situations, and the results show that RIDE can effectively identify hazard scenes and provide practical advice to reduce road accidents.

This research proposes a novel framework for robotics that integrates control barrier functions with optimal control theory to address motion planning challenges, especially those involving unpredictable environments, sensor failures, and control malfunctions. Existing control barrier functions can only provide a minimum time to failure and are not capable of adapting to changes in their dynamic nature. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is developed using a hybrid of optimal control and control barrier functions, allowing for robust time-failure estimation and optimal control simultaneously. A solution to this problem is found through a two-step process, and we demonstrate its efficacy using a hard-to-control robotic system as a test case, showcasing its capabilities in navigating obstacles, avoiding collisions, and withstanding disruptions to state estimation and control.

For a ring with a right (left) identity, denoted as 1, we define enveloping numbers involving countable operations. These numbers are specifically related to sequences of elements multiplied by 1. Research shows that such numbers are either finite or have a specific lower bound infinity, often denoted as $\infty_R$ or $\uparrow$. However, when dealing with associative rings, only the lower bound infinity is relevant. These enveloping numbers form a subadditive continuous ordered monoid under a specific operation. Moreover, we apply the Fuchs-Lavrov theorem to determine the order structure of these enveloping numbers. For non-unital rings, we define enveloping numbers using a specific sequence of matrix-like objects, known as extended sequences. These extended sequences are specifically related to elements of the form $R \times \ldots \times R \to R$, where the size of the sequence can vary. These extended sequences are unique in that the final element can have a specific dependence on the preceding elements, often denoted as $f_{n-1}$ for the $(n-1)$th element. By applying a category theory framework, we define natural transformations between such extended sequences. These natural transformations are unique in that the final element can have a specific dependence on the preceding elements, often denoted as $\Delta f_n=f_{n-1}$. Research shows that such natural transformations are either constant or ultimately dependent sequences, where the final element can have a specific

Understanding and mitigating robustness issues in machine learning models, particularly with regards to adversarial examples, is essential. The ability of these models to generalize effectively beyond their training data is compromised by the very mechanisms that enable them to make predictions. The inherent trade-off between minimizing loss and maintaining predictive classification causes them to also minimize prediction loss, a phenomenon observed in both linear and nonlinear models. This contradiction drives the need for innovative approaches that strike a balance between optimization and generalization goals, ultimately resulting in predictions that resist manipulations and ensure reliable performance in practical applications.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through nonnegative, locally integrable functions over $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ are examined, with a focus on the singular limit of nonlocal to local transition. First, we establish the singular limit for a general class of nonlocal flux functions. Next, we address the issue of entropy admissibility in this singular limit. Finally, we obtain an estimate of the rate of convergence for the solutions to the nonlocal models.

A dilation surface is defined as a compact, orientable two-dimensional manifold equipped with an alternating positive and negative function, where the sign determines whether a point is an extropole or an intropole. A particular type of dilation surface, known as standard, can be constructed from a link diagram via the thickness of its long components. A specific subset of standard dilation surfaces, termed horizon saddle links, are revealed in this research to be in one-to-one correspondence with Reidemeister moves-affected morse-sampling graphs. Furthermore, this study also demonstrates that the isomorphism between two dilation surfaces corresponds to a certain type of homeomorphism that preserves their morse-sampling graphs. As a result, this research establishes a distinct class of dilation surfaces, where the morse-sampling graphs are in inherent equivalence. Using this, the paper's authors successfully identify two distinct, non-isomorphic dilation surfaces with the same morse-sampling graph, but with different topological structures in their morse-sampling graphs. Moreover, these two dilation surfaces can be distinguished via their infinite dilation functions. A particular subset of standard dilation surfaces, known as saddle-free, is revealed in this research to be in one-to-one correspondence with planar, oriented graphs. Using this, the paper's authors successfully resolve the generalization of the open problem posed by Lecouvey by demonstrating that any dilation surface can be transformed into a saddle-free surface via a sequence of certain type of moves.

Recent studies examining resting-state brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging have revealed distinct brain networks. To further explore these networks, researchers have employed measures of correlation between brain regions. Building upon existing work with correlation, this study introduces the use of total correlation to analyze brain activity and function. Total correlation captures complex, multi-variable relationships between regions, offering a more comprehensive insight into brain networks. To illustrate its value, total correlation is applied in two approaches - identifying spatial patterns of high correlation and constructing a brain connectivity graph. These methods are shown to not only conform to established knowledge about brain anatomy but also provide novel insights into brain connectivity. Tractography data from diffusion MRI is used to derive comparisons with white matter brain pathways. Furthermore, principal component analysis is employed to decompose a total correlation matrix, thereby shedding light on key aspects of brain connectivity. To address the challenges of handling large datasets, this study develops an algorithm utilizing Gaussian approximation and blocking techniques to calculate a blocked total correlation matrix. This algorithm is shown to accurately approximate a full correlation matrix while significantly reducing computational demands. To showcase its practical utility, this study calculates a total correlation matrix from fMRI data related to the basal gang-thalamocortical circuit and its relationship with Parkinson's disease.

This study introduces an in-depth exploration of the SB transformation when operating on Clifford algebra-based functions. The SB operator's property of being a Hermitian operator is demonstrated, and a formula is provided for its eigenvalues. The research establishes a relationship, now referred to as the TB isomorphism, which links Clifford algebra-based functions to polynomials on extended, higher-dimensional spaces. The TB isomorphism is shown to be an isomorphism of Hilbert spaces, and its underlying TB eigen equation is identified as a Cauchy-type partial differential equation. Eigenvalue solutions of the SB operator within the context of finite-dimensional Clifford algebras are presented, and these solutions are shown to be linked to Dirac-Morse eigenfunctions through the TB isomorphism. The research concludes by outlining potential avenues for future investigation.

A generalized class of Gaussian processes is called a Gaussian field. In this paper, we establish that a Gaussian field with a specific mean value and correlation function can be reconditioned with a new correlation function, point by point, without disrupting its Gaussian structure. This reconditioning process preserves the field's distribution and any statistical properties it originally possessed. To demonstrate this reconditioning, we provide two methods - one utilising stochastic mean-constriction and the other involving novel applications of functional CLT principles. As an example of this reconditioning process's utility, we show that a Gaussian field's reproductive property is maintained even when the original correlation function has a finite correlation radius.

Ground-and-air sensing technologies offer effective communication in complex environments. The integration of ground and air sensors represents a cooperative sensing model, which, despite its potential, remains underutilized. The connectivity between ground and air sensors offers benefits such as surveillance, disaster relief, and search operations. The development of a wireless interface between ground and air sensors is essential for sensing technologies. The use of drones equipped with RGB cameras allows for the transmission of visual data to ground stations. The process involves identifying targets and adjusting parameters such as altitude, speed, and drone yaw to maintain a stable connection. The optimization of these parameters ensures accurate transmission and efficient sensing. The proposed search-and-link algorithm facilitates the establishment of communication between ground and air sensors.

We are on the cusp of a breakthrough in neutrino research that will allow us to
confront fundamental questions about neutrino oscillations, their behavior at
high energies, and interactions in precise detail. The next-generation Deep
 Underground Neutrino Experiment's (DUNE) massive 8-ton Super-K proton target
and 8-times larger detector size than current leading projects ensure we will
reach crucial turning points in neutrino physics, capable of handling high-
precision measurements and massive data sets. With 6 times more neutrino interactions detected and an enormous increase in potenceial event rate, DUNE is well-positioned to solve the persistent identification issue with which current projects struggle, and an independent study has shown the potential of DUNE to resolve the long-standing 13 meV (6σ) square mass difference discrepancy between its capabilities and existing data on neutrino oscillations.

Improving tagged jets, particularly top jets, is crucial for accurate measurements and extraction of physics beyond the Standard Model in complex environments. We present a novel top tagging technique utilizing machine learning, trained on fully integrated collider data. Unlike traditional approaches, this method educates the network simultaneously about tag probabilities and four-momentum resolutions of tagged particles using a combined categorical-cross-entropy loss function. The new algorithm outperforms its predecessors and we explain its improvements using a formal technique that uncovers a latent variable governing tag probabilities. By treating tagging problems as statistical experiments with various signal and background densities at the sub-jet and jet-level, we applied the SHAP method to decompose the multi-variable decision function and determined relative importance factors known as Shapley values. These values were then used to train a smaller, more interpretable tree-based tagging algorithm and shed light on the distinct roles of soft and hard components in tagging jets.

This document establishes the fundamental concepts related to Virtual Organizations and Virtual Organization Replications, serving as a foundation for further research in the field of self-engineering and replications. We have formally derived the mathematical definitions of these concepts from the advanced VO features outlined in [1]. The primary goal of this statement is to validate the fundamental structures of VO and VO Replication, ensuring that they conform to established principles of formalization and are ready for application in the theories of Virtual Organizations and Virtual Organization Replications.

Efficient exploration and data analysis are crucial elements in finding optimal policies in complex environments. Through successful interaction and reward-based learning, agents can improve their understanding of their surroundings and extract valuable information from their experiences. In the context of reinforcement learning, capitalizing on previously collected data, specifically past interactions, can significantly boost the efficiency of training. In this study, we introduce VERO, a novel algorithm that leverages past experiences to facilitate robust and efficient policy optimization. VERO accentuates rewarding outcomes in the policy optimization process by incorporating a time-weighted average of Q-values. Additionally, it accentuates the novelty of observations during sampling, promoting more exploratory behavior. Theoretical and empirical analyses demonstrate that VERO's impact on the maximum entropy reinforcement learning framework leads to better exploration and a more focused attention on less visited states.

Two new methods, the superbosonization of a fermionic action and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, are employed to add a bosonic layer to a fermionic quadratic action. We demonstrate that these approaches yield identical results for the bosonic term added, the source, and the average action when applied to a fermionic action. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the superbosonization method often proves easier to apply than the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, particularly when dealing with fermionic actions featuring nonquadratic terms, which are commonly encountered in practical scenarios.

This paper presents a novel extension to Recurrent Neural Networks, designed to process intricate information about motion over time in sequences of spatiotemporal data. The method, MoDeRNN, prioritizes managing the inherent complexity involved in analyzing such data within the context of recurrent learning. We propose a set of key performance indicators, derived from kinetic energy and angular momentum, to facilitate a systematic approach to motion analysis. These optimized indicators serve to not only alleviate the issue of data scarcity but also to reduce computational complexity involved in their collection. We then integrate the utilization of indicator data into a method of recurrent learning, along with a corresponding decoder for predicting the future state of systems from the obtained indicators. We test the efficacy of this approach on data from the Measuring Wind Tunnel Laboratory at Politecnica di Milano, utilized to analyze the aerodynamic characteristics of an automobile model, along with wind velocities in open environments. The findings indicate that MoDeRNN surpasses traditional RNN models in predictive accuracy and effectively manages computational costs by minimizing the need for data within the training dataset.

This research aims to examine memory safety in the context of distributed systems, focusing on a novel approach incorporating both Rust's ownership and borrowing system and the distributed object runtime (DOR) framework. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed, consisting of existing literature review and empirical analysis. The study evaluates the DOR framework's performance under various memory safety configurations and the effectiveness of incorporating static analysis tools. Furthermore, the research explores the challenges of the current DOR architecture in terms of memory safety and identifies opportunities for improvement in the context of distributed systems.

Investigations into neutrinoless double-beta decay serve as a crucial indicator for fundamental properties of neutrinos and their interactions. In this context, we examine postulated colliders that can generate significant amounts of neutrino-less states in certain particles, for example, the $Z'$ boson. The focus lies in the interplay between Majorana states formed by neutrinos and other particles involved, for example, electron, muon, and $Z$ bosons. The interplay gives rise to an array of $Z'$ models that can be tested through searches at the Large Hadron Collider, especially for a $Z'$ boson decaying into pairs of neutralinos. The $Z'$ masses and couplings that make certain models compatible with constraints from naturalness and other indicators, for example, the Weinberg angle, and muon anomalous magnetic moment, are also discussed.

A proposed iterative decoding method for polar codes leverages subcodes formed by polar subcodes to facilitate iterative decoding through multiple stages. Each stage utilizes belief propagation list decoding to derive the subcode, accompanied by a density evolution calculation to determine the optimal iteration count. The framework's structure allows for Belief Propagation List Decoding to be executed in a variety of sequences, resulting in some instances reaching the maximum probability of error under infinite signal-to-noise ratio conditions. The framework's performance was evaluated and tested against other polar code decoding methods in several simulation scenarios.

This paper examines the characteristics of point spread functions (PSFs) resulting from combining multiple astronomical images. The study considers the outcomes for various types of PSFs, including Gaussian, Laguerre-Gaussian, and Zernike polynomials. The research focuses on the diffraction-limited point spread functions of astronomical telescopes and the techniques used to combine multiple images through adaptive calibration or algorithms. The outcomes for different combinations of image numbers and arrangements are calculated and presented. The study further explores the applications and limitations of these combined PSFs and suggests that they could be useful for low-resolution image reconstruction, astrometry, and other astronomical applications.

The fracture strength of materials depends on how well they can absorb stress before it reaches their critical fracture point. Several studies, including those of Kitagawa and Matsunaga, among others, have explored the effect of pre-existing cracks on the fracture strength of metals. These studies found that the fracture strength of metals decreases as the size of the crack increases. However, there are significant variations in the fracture strength of different metals. Moreover, there are considerable differences in the way fracture strength is affected by cracks in metals and in the fracture strength of crystals. It has been observed that the fracture strength of crystals decreases as the size of the crack increases at a slower rate than it does in metals. The fracture strength of metals typically decreases in the order: Cu, Al, Ag, Au, whereas the fracture strength of crystals decreases in the order: NaCl, KCl, KBr, KBr:Na. The fracture strength of crystals increases with an increase in temperature, but the fracture strength of metals decreases with an increase in temperature. The energy absorbed per unit volume at fracture in metals and in sodium chloride is investigated.

We examine the relationship between the half-plane free field's correlation function and multiple SLEs driven by multiple independent Brownian motions. Firstly, we place multiple SLEs within the half-plane and obtain the corresponding observables. These need to satisfy a certain stochastic partial differential equation. We resolve this equation using the methods and results from [DPS18], [PS19], [PZ20], as well as Conformal Field Theory. We establish the convergence of the multiple SLE observables towards those of the Gaussian free field, by matching them with the field whose correlation function we earlier derived at the convergence limit of the multiple Brownian motions' life times to the half-plane's correlation function. This achieves a full characterisation of the limit based on a multiple SLE setup rather than the multiple Gaussian free fields. A prior work by Dub\'e and Schenkel [DS20] also addresses this, employing a dual approach. We compare and integrate our findings with theirs.

We consider the three-dimensional periodic Novier-Stokes equations for an incompressible fluid with a smooth initial velocity field. This study provides the strongest known a priori estimates related to the velocity and vorticity of solutions. Specifically, estimates are expressed in terms of the maximum value of the Sobolev norm and the Strichartz norm of the velocity, ultimately leading to the existence of local and global solutions. These solutions exhibit temporary or permanent loss of regularity, characterized by a decrease in the Sobolev norm or the emergence of singularities in the vorticity.

The increasing reliance on quantum computing requires development and deployment methods that can reliably guarantee correct outcomes. However, ensuring the accuracy of these complex systems poses significant challenges due to the inherent complexity of verifying quantum states and their gates. This complexity barrier has hindered widespread adoption of quantum systems, prompting a need for efficient verification tools. This study introduces an innovative, time-efficient approach to validate quantum gate sets based on conventional logic principles. This novel method reduces the verification time associated with state validation in line with linear time complexity, making it feasible for large-scale applications. The proposed solution leverages hybrid classical-quantum computing techniques and incorporates hybrid CNF-DNF formulae to optimize the approach. This innovative method outperforms existing linear-time verification solutions by leveraging fine-grained unitarity and ignoring irrelevant qubit details.

A blockchain system allows Tanner-Infra, LLC and others to create a reliable and secure framework for Internet of Things (IoT) networks. This framework can be applied to various industries including healthcare, transportation, and logistics by utilizing a distributed ledger technology (DLT). Our proposed framework uses a modular approach consisting of a central DLT, IoT devices, 5G technology, a blockchain platform, and an oracle and smart contract infrastructure. The oracle and smart contract infrastructure enables flexible DLT integration with external systems. The framework's effectiveness was demonstrated through a proof-of-concept pilot involving a food supply chain.

Our goal is to develop a method to automatically generate various cell forms using a training approach based on reinforcement learning. Since characterizing a cell's shape can be highly complex, with properties such as irregular surfaces and intricate details, traditional image recognition techniques are not suitable. Instead, we utilize function representations to encode cell images and develop a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that adjusts the function representation to produce diverse cell images. The success of our approach relies on a proposed criterion that measures the distance between our generated images and target cell images using their respective function representations. Extensive experiments confirm that our method successfully trains to produce a range of cell forms and, when tested on new data, generalizes accurately. Notably, the function representations learned through our method are versatile, allowing for multiple, novel cell forms to be generated through various mixing techniques applied to the training data. These advantages of our method, which includes its ability to efficiently handle complex shapes and generate diverse cell forms, could be applied to other image classification and generation challenges.

Document accessibility for readers with print disabilities is a critical issue.
Researchers have primarily focused on accessible documents for readers with disabilities to read digitally, but overlooked the needs of print-impaired individuals who struggle with physical or chemical disabilities in processing information. These individuals rely on human assistance to access documents, specifically highlighting key sections which then gets transferred into braille or audio formats. To address this, a new concept of document navigability is introduced, which encompasses the necessary features to facilitate human assistance. A collaborative research approach was employed to identify the required elements of document navigality. Through interviews with visually impaired individuals, their scribes, and highlighters, researchers determined that documents should provide clear divisions of content, marked annotations, designated images with text translations, and detailed metadata that includes an official endorsement of document navigality, accompanied with helpful supportive features such as highlighted annotations, translated alt-text for images, and integrated metadata. An online survey with 318 participants confirmed that the proposed definition of document navigality aligns with the needs and preferences of print-impaired individuals. The researchers further determined that the proposed document navigality features can be implemented at a relatively low additional cost, specifically an estimated $13 million per year for the United States book industry. The study suggests that the incorporation of document navigality as an industry standard is feasible and would greatly benefit print-impaired individuals.

While BERT excels at handling bidirectional contexts through bidirectional transformers, its training relies on the directionality of language structure, which leads to inefficient use of autoregressive modeling. To address this limitation, we've developed a new pretraining strategy for language understanding. Our approach, XLNet, has evolved from the ERNIE algorithm and incorporates elide-and-recover technique to handle bidirectional contextual information in a novel way. Moreover, XLNet employs arithmetic operations on permutations of BERT's self-attention, thereby enhancing the model's ability to sample tokens and train it in an autoregressive manner. Our experiments show that XLNet outperforms BERT and RoBERTa on 20 out of 30 benchmarks.

We have created computational models to analyze how stellar activity affects spectroscopic analysis in exoplanet research, specifically transit spectroscopy, using real data from stars AD Leo and EV Lac to test low and high-resolution settings. Our study reveals that to accurately determine atmospheric properties of exoplanets using transit spectroscopy, stellar activity must be minimized, typically below 10% of the solar activity level. Achieving this requires data resolution of at least 30,000. Under this resolution threshold, stellar activity overwhelms signals from the exoplanet and masks its characteristics. Using simulated data, our research demonstrates that to detect water on an exoplanet similar to Earth, we must suppress stellar activity to levels seen in very quiet main-sequence stars like Proxima Centauri or the Sun in its current state. In theory, solar-like activity could mask water presence on exoplanets for decades, rendering incorrect low-resolution spectroscopic readings. High-resolution settings are essential for validating water detection and understanding solar system analogues.

This paper focuses on developing a metric with uniform curvature on a Riemann surface containing singularities. Initially, a conformal metric with this characteristic is created on a compact Riemann surface free of singularities. Subsequently, the paper presents two approaches to extend this notion to Riemann surfaces with singularities. The first method relies on a recent study by the authors, which established a relationship between the existence of a Green function on a Riemann surface and its compactification. The second approach adapts a previous argument by Troyansky, who employed a similar strategy to investigate the existence of a Green function on a Riemann surface with singularities. The paper also includes a review of the established results on the existence of Green functions on such surfaces.

Research into the locomotion of centipedes when moving across water-surfaces suggests a conventional view that these creatures employ an alternating movement of their body parts to create a wave-like action may not be accurate for species that are extremely light-weight. Instead, our measurements reveal a different wave pattern where the alternating movement of the centipede's body segments is less consistent, directly related to the speed of the creature and the frequency of its leg movements. A new theoretical model that takes into consideration the light-weight of these creatures has allowed us to better understand and quantify the wave pattern, the efficiency of their movement and how their speed is directly related to the frequency of their leg movements.

The ultimate goal of this project is to develop highly advanced computer models that can accurately simulate and predict the intricate processes involved in a tsunami triggered by a massive ocean impact, including its dispersal and the formation of unusual wave patterns. This ambitious goal demands an unprecedented level of computational precision, specifically at the level of rounding errors in the used algorithms, an analysis of which has already revealed potential issues with the method. In order to achieve our objective, we are implementing a precise numerical model of the N-body problem and integrating it with the existing hydrodynamic code based on the volume-of-control-element method. This integration model accounts for key factors such as the formation of solitary waves and run-up in the shallow-water equation. In future phases, we will incorporate additional essential elements, such as atmospheric effects and dispersion caused by ocean currents and eddies.

Recent surveys using ALMA and SPICA/PLATO have identified a population of strongly infrared-luminous galaxies that are not visible in optically focused surveys. These galaxies are likely to be a significant component of the cosmic infrared background radiation. New data from the James Webb Space Telescope is allowing researchers to study these galaxies in greater detail across the ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum. These new observations include 32 galaxies that were selected from the ALMA/IRAS 6 $\mu$m sample, which showed strong emission features characteristic of dust-obscured galaxies. Analysis of these galaxies using spectral energy distribution models reveals that they are predominantly low-to-intermediate redshift galaxies with high stellar masses and strong dust obscuration. Despite their large stellar masses, these galaxies are not among the closest local galaxies and are largely composed of two distinct galaxy types: massive star-forming galaxies similar to M82-likes and dwarf irregular galaxies similar to IC10. Spectral features in the near-infrared spectrum indicate the presence of AGB stars and a large fraction of dust-obscured galaxies, which aligns with the findings from ALMA observations. These galaxies are significantly more massive and densely star-forming than typical local dwarf galaxies, which are thought to be the local analogs of these galaxies at higher redshifts. These findings are significant because they suggest that massive star-forming and dwarf irregular galaxies in the local universe are not representative of these galaxy types in the early universe.
