A robust commercial driving system relies on well-informed decision-making to maintain high standards of customer satisfaction, maintain industry and legal compliance, and mitigate risks associated with poor decisions. To achieve this, a decision-support system was designed to help human experts make more informed choices, particularly in situations where there were doubts about the capabilities of automated decision-making systems. By testing the system in a real-world context, researchers compared the decision-making abilities of both artificial intelligence and human experts in real-time to identify which was more accurate in predicting successful outcomes. Following the implementation of the system, researchers found that it led to an overall 15% higher scores for three key performance indicators compared to before, while also revealing that there was no significant difference in the prediction abilities of both artificial intelligence and human experts. However, by incorporating human expertise, the system was able to enhance the accuracy of artificial intelligence outputs, ultimately resulting in better decision-making outcomes for customers.

The Out-of-Category challenge held during the ACM Multimedia 2021 conference aimed to 1)  assess the ability of models to handle out-of-category data, which is crucial for developing practical multimedia applications, and 2)  understand the effect of out-of-category data on model performance. The challenge featured two tracks: a retrieval task in which models categorized data without annotations, and a classification task with explicit annotations. On the retrieval side, results showed that transformer-based models handle out-of-category data better than their deep metric learning counterparts. The classification task revealed that out-of-category data can both improve and decrease model performance. Additionally, we discovered that the impact of out-of-category data varies across multimedia types and tasks.

This research investigates the geometric properties of minima in multi-dimensional random fields that adhere to a Gaussian distribution, considering these fields as surfaces within higher-dimensional space. We identify a specific criterion that distinguishes optimal geometric paths on these surfaces, whether they are straight lines or curved paths, by controlling the maximal angle between these paths and the local tangent planes at various points. Our study provides thresholds for this angle in one-dimensional and multi-dimensional fields with multiple local minima. Moreover, our field has applications in understanding the optimization of certain multi-dimensional random functions, such as polynomial functions and linear combinations of higher-order moments.
This note outlines a different approach to Demoures and Gong's work on counting repeated subblocks within words, utilizing a graphical method that reveals a periodic pattern.

For a Hecke cusp form, let $L(s)$ be its associated Dirichlet series modified Hecke cusp form and $\tau$ be the Szego-Boltzmann invariant. The work of Iwanec and Saha reveals that the rational roots of $L(1+it)/\tau$ are uniquely bounded between two numbers, one always positive and the other positive only for roots of odd order. This discussion extends the work of Iwanec and Saha by providing a simplified proof and simultaneously broadens the scope to include all $L(s)$ and $\tau$-functions. The argument demonstrates that the rational roots of $L(1+it)$ and $\tau$ are distinctively bounded between two numbers, with one always greater and the other always less than a specific number, for all orders. The discussion concludes by predicting bounded roots for Dirichlet L-functions and potentially various other L-functions.

In a study on spin transport in armchair graphene nanoribbons with thin layers of hexagonal boron nitride, it was observed that the spin resolution can be manipulated using gate voltage, regardless of the ribbons' orientation. This transport mechanism, however, strongly depends on the ribbons' width, and a method to control spin resolution was developed. Research found that the spin resolution can be improved by reducing the ribbons' width, and demonstrated that the spin resolution can be fully cancelled out using gate voltage in ribbons of a specific width. This discovery enabled the development of a more precise method to control spin currents through graphene nanoribbon technology.

The Korovkin theorem, initially applied to multivariate functions with certain properties, guarantees the almost everywhere convergence of a class of linear operators acting on multivariate functions to a specific form. This paper, however, presents an extension of this concept to functions with weak nonlinearities that meet certain conditions, including those involving convexity. The results presented have far-reaching implications, covering a wide range of nonlinear approximation methods that meet specific conditions, such as being monotone and continuous. The proof presented offers significant advantages over existing methodologies in the field, including approximation by convex functions. The results presented, therefore, encompass and strengthen multiple existing theorem and proof types, including those by approximation by convex functions, nonlinear approximation methods, and the Korovkin theorem itself.

We develop a general framework for deriving Hamiltonian properties of graphs given specific conditions on their vertex independence numbers. This method has the following key benefits: the bounds obtained are tight; the approach can be applied to various graph problems beyond Hamiltonian. Leveraging our technique, we identify a precise threshold for the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle in graphs of a specific type and apply this result to develop a more refined estimate for a related graph parameter. Additionally, we utilize our method to demonstrate a condition under which a graph contains multiple pairwise disjoint Hamiltonian cycles.

We analyzed the directed flow of charged particles from the STAR experiment at RHIC.  Our analysis covered Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and a novel combination of Ru+Ru and CuCu collisions at a high energy level.  We observed that, unlike light nuclei collisions which showed a change in directed flow dependence on centrality, individual species of hadrons exhibited distinct directed flow patterns that varied with centrality, a result which deviated from our initial assumption of universal directed flow across all species within centrality ranges.  Furthermore, our data revealed a decline in directed flow of all charged particles as energy per participant nucleon increased, while selected particle groups, such as protons and antiprotons, displayed varying behavior in this regard.  Lastly, our findings showed no detectable difference in directed flow between Ru+Ru and Cu+Cu collisions at similar participant numbers.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex dynamical systems by utilizing Koopman operator theory to simplify a system's representation. This method works by representing complex, non-orthogonal system eigenfunctions through an optimal set of basis functions. These basis functions were initially guessed as initial value problems and then optimized using a multivariate dimension reduction technique based on its stability properties. To improve computational efficiency, a proposed method integrates the ASK method with a sparse grid technique to select crucial basis functions from an extensive set of Smolyak structured combinatorics. This integration results in a more efficient and reliable ASK method for solving large-scale systems within a short time frame and at high resolution.

This research explores the numerical behavior of the unique outer complex scaling approach in solving the Schrödinger equation for an electron in a strong linear DC electric field interacting with a nucleus of a hydrogen-like atom. The method relies on the complex scaling potential to decouple the continuum states from the bound states in variable scaling parameters. The study examines the behavior of the Hamiltonian in different superposition states without employing the linear potential approximation for the Coulomb interaction. The results, obtained from a multi-energy approach, demonstrate the accuracy of the method in different non-Born-Oppenheimer states and highlight their potential applications in theoretical spectroscopy and chemistry. The outcomes also show the outer complex scaling method's efficacy in scenarios where the nucleus and electron overlap.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used for solving the Sinkhorn problem, which involves finding the optimal transport map between two probability distributions within a metric space, under the constraint of conservation of mass. It's known that this algorithm always converges to a stationary point under the condition that mass is preserved. However, in cases where conservation of mass is not possible due to a negative Schrodinger eigenvalue, the algorithm may not reach a solution. In such situations, we demonstrate that the algorithm converges towards a set of points that cannot be considered solutions to the transport problem. Additionally, we show that these limiting points are in fact stationary points of the Sinkhorn divergence, which may not necessarily align with the conservative mass constraint. This study highlights a critical issue in mass transportation that has significant implications across various fields.

Results from measuring the total cross-section of $t\bar{t}$ events using the ATLAS detector at the LHC are presented. The data used in the analysis comprises a total of 254 ns of pooled data from 2017 and 2018 datasets, each recorded at a proton-proton collision energy of 5.02 TeV and with an integrated luminosity of 25.4 fb$^{-1}$. The $t\bar{t}$ cross-section was assessed through single-lepton and double-lepton decay modes that account for 94% of $t\bar{t}$ events. The measurement's results indicate a $t\bar{t}$ cross-section of 67.5 pb, aligning perfectly with theoretical Standard Model predictions of 85.7 pb, presenting a modest 19% deviation.

We're studying transport behavior in a model of many particles that interact through a central link. This link enables direct communication, regardless of spatial distance, and facilitates the exchange of information. This complex of interacting particles is a key component in various scientific disciplines and emerging research areas, including quantum chemistry, quantum optics, and traffic modeling. By analyzing how particles detach from the central link, as well as the effects of coupling strength and number of particles, we've gained insight into the underlying localization behavior in this model. Our research focuses on the critical point where the central link collapses and the resulting spatial localizations of particles take place. By identifying this critical point at six particles, as indicated by numerical calculations, we've demonstrated its dependence on the coupling strength and explored the resulting phase transition in this model. Furthermore, we've analyzed the spatial localizations of particles in different phases through numerical calculations and theoretical models, which has led to the identification of two types of localization phases: weak and strong. These phases are distinguished by the position of the effective mass parameter relative to the coupling strength and the number of particles. If the effective mass is less than the coupling strength, the phase is strong, resulting in weak coupling between particles; otherwise, the phase is weak, with strong coupling between particles. This two-phase structure has been confirmed to be stable against various particle arrangements and discussed in relation to the resulting spatial structures.

The convexity properties of a function involving generalized Bessel functions are examined, specifically looking at subclasses of Janowski's class. Conditions on these functions, tied to their power series, are provided and proven.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, city dwellers exhibited distinct mobility patterns influenced by socioeconomic factors, resulting in a more uneven spatial dispersion of high and low interactions among diverse population groups compared to pre-pandemic levels of interaction. Analysis of mobility data from mobile devices in three diverse urban settings in North America and Europe reveals this phenomenon. Prior research indicated a natural disparity in interaction frequency among lower and higher socioeconomic city dwellers before the pandemic, but an abrupt shift in government policies in early 2020 significantly amplified these disparities, leading to a substantial increase in differences in interaction probability among various socioeconomic groups by 2.6 to 3.8 times, depending on the city. This significant amplification is attributed to individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds adopting risk-averse behaviors, such as enhanced stay-at-home activities and reduced social engagement, resulting in further marginalization of already isolated segments of the population. Furthermore, a parallel increase in government intervention also revealed a limited capacity to mitigate socioeconomic disparities in interaction frequency. By combining demographic and socioeconomic data with spatial network models, our research gains insights into the intricate relationships between government policies, socioeconomic factors, and urban social interactions.

There's a pressing need to speed up simulations of complex two-phase flows in the petroleum industry. To achieve this, researchers have developed various strategies to divide the simulation field into smaller parts without changing the fundamental equations governing the problem. In numerical terms, dividing the simulation field into smaller parts enables faster computation of the same complex system. A key aspect of dividing the simulation field into smaller parts involves minimizing data exchange between these divisions, which becomes increasingly challenging when the divisions change size. In this study, different methods for dividing the simulation field into smaller parts, specifically linear and non-linear methods, are investigated for a specific type of porous medium. A comparison of these methods shows that non-linear division methods offer significant advantages and can significantly reduce the need to exchange data and/or change the size of divisions, resulting in substantial speed-up of simulations. Ultimately, the best approach for dividing the simulation field into smaller parts depends on the specific type of porous medium and what characteristics are prioritized (e.g. accuracy or speed).

The property of circular birefringence originates from the different refractive indices experienced by left and right circularly rotating electric fields. Traditionally, it is implemented through a circularly symmetric structure. This research proposes a new method to produce a unidirectional optical birefringence phenomenon using a non-circular resonator. This concept is demonstrated within a modified elliptical microdisk resonator. The single-handedness chiral properties are analyzed using fundamental physical principles. These principles allow for the prediction of specific resonance frequencies and their corresponding rotation speeds. The proposed method has potential in developing efficient and compact devices for optical rotation, which could be used in various applications such as verifiable data storage and quantum information processing.

This study specifically examines the gravitational limit of Liouville CFT, incorporating gravitational dressing for Virasoro vertex operators, resulting in a well-known limit that yields the free scalar CFT describing free bosons on a semi-circle. We develop an alternative approach to achieve this limit by embedding Liouville CFT within a supersymmetric CFT, involving a specific coupling for its stress tensor. This embedding allows for an explicit calculation of the gravitational dressing terms. Subsequently, we verify that the gravitational action, including the associated flux boundary term, exhibits conformal invariance. Notably, the studied model bears resemblance to a specific mini-superstring model described by Kang and Maldacena.

This article explores various solutions for an ideal fluid in the context of Generalized Maxwell's equations, specifically the warp drive configuration. By considering three different cases - with and without the cosmological constant and accounting for its potential sign - we derive potential warp drive solutions. These solutions include two cases without the cosmological constant, which result in a straightforward velocity distribution, and a constant-c curvature case that yields a warp drive configuration with the cosmological constant present.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require increasing maintenance, cities face challenges in reducing costs and risks while ensuring infrastructure reliability. Construction and maintenance companies face further complications due to the lack of accurate mapping data, causing them to rely on guesswork. However, a recent breakthrough in sensing technology and data analysis offers cities the opportunity to update their underground mapping. 

This study introduces an innovative solution to address this need by combining various data sources using a specific processing technique to create detailed, accurate maps. The proposed system consists of two components: a central database to store and manage spatial data and an algorithmic module to analyze this data and generate a consistent map. 

The development of this solution involved utilizing various city documents and creating a model to address the specific needs of underground mapping, given the limitations of available data. The proposed system was then tested on a real-world dataset and compared to alternative approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness and time efficiency. 

The study also highlights the potential applications and advantages of this solution, including its feasibility and adaptability to a wide range of scenarios, making it a valuable resource for infrastructure data maintenance.

To study the effects of motional states in 2D ion crystals, we're using the Y$_2$-Y lattice arrangement with $^{168}$Y ions and investigating how the Y ions' spin interactions are affected by their movement between lattice sites. The Y ions' spin interactions create a shared spin state that can be examined through the application of two different types of pulses. The Y ions' motion contributes to the spread of this shared spin state in a manner dependent on the ions' relative motion temperatures. The observed rate of spin interaction degradation is higher than what would be predicted if the Y ions were in a state of uniform motion at a specific temperature. This indicates that a broader range of motional states exists, and to achieve a complete understanding, it's necessary to consider a distribution of motional states rather than a single uniform temperature. The observed rate of spin interaction degradation can be matched with a model that accounts for a Gaussian distribution of motional states. The model reveals that higher velocities of heating are required to explain the observed rate of spin interaction degradation. The found maximum velocities of ion movement agree with the expected rate of movement in a two-dimensional crystal arrangement. The studied method provides a means to measure the temperature and velocity distribution of ion movements within two-dimensional crystal structures. The found velocity distribution may also be employed in other modes of trapping and for species that exhibit varied trapping behaviors.

TERS is an advanced spectroscopic technique providing local spatial information, though its signal origin remains a current debate. The current implementation relies on complex light distribution simulations within chemical groups and moieties. The associated models are mainly based on classical assumptions regarding electromagnetic interactions between molecules and the surrounding environment. Consequently, the lack of a thorough quantum treatment is felt. In our approach, an ab initio method has been developed, which includes a comprehensive quantum model for light-matter interactions in TERS. The results of our simulation reveal a good agreement with experimental data. The findings confirm that the specific arrangement of chemical groups in a sample influences its light concentration pattern. The presented quantum model offers a new approach to understanding local electromagnetic effects in TERS, complementing existing models. The proposed method can serve as a useful tool for analyzing TERS data and identifying specific chemical groups within a sample.

We conducted K-band observations of 19 galaxies near our Milky Way using the Sardinia Radio Telescope's real-time capabilities to search for synthetic microwave background radiation, focusing on sources with temperatures above 20 mK. Our findings revealed one galaxy, NGC 4567, exhibiting a potential excess at 24.5 GHz with a measured intensity equivalent to 120.5(19.4-57.6) mJy. Intensity values for other galaxies, including NGC 4570, NGC 4571, and NGC 4654, showed excess signals at various frequencies but within the 5 sigma confidence level. These results are being submitted for confirmation through follow-up observations.

Results from theoretical calculations using first-principles electronic structure approaches, specifically ab initio molecular dynamics and density functional theory, are presented for the analysis of ammonium sulfate ferroelectricity. These findings reveal that the heat capacity maximum corresponds to a substantial entropy increase associated with ferroelectric phase transition heat. Utilizing phonon and electronic temperature-dependent property calculations, the origin of this entropy peak is investigated and divided into contributions from vibrational, electronic, and spin-related entropy components. Observations indicate that the vibrational component dominates the entropy increase peaked at 26 K, while the electronic and spin-related components significantly contribute to lower temperature ranges. These computational outcomes are compared with experimental entropy data, showcasing the model's capability and completeness in describing the system's behavior.

Significant research has highlighted the role of the brain's dopaminergic midbrain in learning through rewards and penalties. Past studies revealed that individuals using optimal reinforcement learning strategies learn more efficiently and accurately, and that suboptimal strategies might be an indication of midbrain dysfunction. However, the relationship between midbrain function and the use of suboptimal strategies remains unclear. In our investigation, participants viewed films and assigned rewards or penalties based on their emotions, either adopting an optimal or suboptimal approach to prediction. Compared to optimal strategies, suboptimal strategies were consistently associated with decreased prediction error signals in the midbrain and lower-than-expected accuracy rates. Notably, when compared to a control group, participants using suboptimal strategies showed increased emotional intensity. In cases where learning from penalties was difficult due to pre-existing emotional biases, the midbrain's prediction error signals suggested a greater struggle between expected and actual outcomes. These results indicate that midbrain dysfunction may lead to the development of suboptimal strategies, and suggest a possible link between emotion regulation and the use of reinforcement learning tactics.

In research, we investigate quantum entanglement and contextuality using 
the E8 (Einstein-rosen) core system's complexifications by introducing extra dimensions.
We generate two types of entangled states, and our analysis indicates that both types 
can be detected with single-qubit measurements. Additionally, we create a set of mutually 
unentangleable groups using complexifications of E8. Our findings suggest that complexifying 
any core system may lead to a contextually rich and potentially quantum entangled state.

The challenge of finding near neighbors within a dataset is crucial in domains such as multimedia search, leveraging its time series component for tasks like retrieving similar gesture or movement patterns. For two curves, the Frechet distance measures the level of alignment and similarity between them. Specifically, it assesses the degree to which they avoid crossing each other. In our investigation, we explored near neighbor search in datasets containing rigid motion time series, all of the same duration, employing the Frechet distance as the metric. Our goal focused on developing an algorithm that can efficiently return a limited number of the most similar series. Notably, we proved that any method capable of returning all nearest neighbors within a dataset of $n$ motion series and a query time series of $t$, while ensuring an $\epsilon$ approximation bound, would require a minimum of $\Omega(t^{3/4}\cdot n^{1/2})$ time. Furthermore, we achieved this bound by demonstrating an algorithm capable of producing the same results. By utilizing our technique, we demonstrated the possibility of reducing the time complexity of solving the $\delta$-Frechet Distance problem to $O((\delta)^{7/3}\cdot n^{1/2})$ time, representing an improvement of several orders of magnitude over existing solutions.

To achieve accurate measurements in quantum physics, quantum sensors, and other advanced technologies, the distortion caused by limited precision instruments must be addressed. Current methods for correcting such distortions often struggle with issues like high computational requirements, the limitation of processing a single batch of data at a time, and the need for precise knowledge of the instrument's performance. To overcome these challenges, we have developed Scalable Measurement Error Correction (SMEC), an iterative process that corrects measurement errors. SMEC requires only general knowledge of the instrument and can correct complex types of distortions. It also allows us to process larger data sets, analyze individual data points, and applies to a broader range of distortions beyond quantum-related ones. SMEC has been successfully tested using simulated data for scenarios involving up to 1 million data points and various types of distortions.

As autonomous robots navigate diverse environments to accomplish complex tasks, they need to interact with numerous individuals who will encounter them in their daily lives. To effectively navigate these interactions, robots must convey their intentions and capabilities through communication. To achieve this, we introduce the Human-Robot Interaction Scale, a 28-item scale measuring how humans respond to robotic communications. We developed this scale by combining existing communication theories, such as the Social Learning Theory and Theory of Mental States, and testing it in an experiment with human subjects. In the experiment, participants interacted with a robot capable of navigating around obstacles and anticipating their actions. In a collaborative task, the robot's navigation helped participants reach a higher reward compared to the robot's non-verbal counterparts. In addition to the Human-Robot Interaction Scale, we observed that human satisfaction with the interactions increased when the robot explained its actions using mentalistic language, such as "I think you'll like it better this way." This suggests that humans value robots that demonstrate an understanding of their thoughts and perspectives.

For tasks such as planetary exploration, rescue missions, and cartography, creating detailed maps is essential. Unfortunately, existing map types like topographic maps and graphs fail to combine the benefits of topological and geometric information efficiently. Topological maps, particularly Minimum Spanning Trees and Hierarchical Graphs, offer valuable topological structure but struggle with geometric representation, hindering navigation and local orientation. Conversely, planar networks and Cellular Automata provide ample geometric information but compromise topological clarity. In response, we introduce HiTMap, a novel map representation that caters to the needs of users navigating unknown environments. Comprising a hierarchical structure of MFTs and HTs, each level reflects the varying scales of the environment. By prioritizing topological precision at the HT level and incorporating geometric details at the MFT level, HiTMap enables clear navigation and map understanding. Furthermore, our indoor-outdoor classification system enables the detection of ambient conditions from the global environmental perspective. Through our global mapping system's internal view, an octree data structure ensures that the sub-map of the local environment is efficiently stored, allowing for accurate metrics of the remaining unvisited areas. In our experimental analysis, we compare the performance of our proposed system with established topological and geometric representations, demonstrating that HiTMap reduces the speed of arrivals for navigation, orientation, and map understanding by 35%, 15%, and 12% respectively.

Conventional two-dimensional arrays with supplementary codes, developed from Boolean functions, are confined to four possible values. In this paper, a novel two-dimensional array code with supplementary values is proposed, derived from multivariable functions that can accommodate eight possible values. These functions are characterized by eight possible output states and are highly flexible, making them suitable for coding. Based on multivariable functions, an inter-group complementary code set and 2-D Z-supplementary array code set are designed, exhibiting several desirable properties including fixed-length sequences, variable-length sequences, eight possible values, and strict two-dimensional array relationships. Further, two-dimensional arrays with supplementary codes are applied in sequence alignment to demonstrate their utility in correcting single-bit errors and illustrating time-saving potential in sequences where there are few zeros. Due to their ability to accommodate eight possible values, multivariable functions-based two-dimensional arrays with supplementary codes offer a range of potential applications in coding theory and practice.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a widely employed imaging technique that utilizes the attenuation of X-rays by various materials to generate images. Traditional CT scans typically utilize a single energy level (monochromatic) and rely on a limited set of materials to create a reconstructed image. However, this method has its limitations, especially in situations involving multiple materials, where misclassifications may result in distorted image reconstructions. To address these issues, we introduce a novel variational framework utilizing multiple energy sources (polyenergetic source CT) to improve image quality and material identification. Our framework not only enhances image reconstructions, but also accurately separates and identifies materials by decomposing sensor data and automatically selecting the optimal number of materials through a technique known as hypersphere clustering. Our method includes a trainable neural network component that can be used for a range of tasks. To prevent overfitting, our framework incorporates a data denoising mechanism, utilizing a GAN. Our method was tested using actual polyenergetic data from a few sources and a specially created phantom with a variety of materials.

We investigate the behavior of gap plasmons as the gap width approaches zero, using an electron gas model that takes into account an electron spill-out into the gap and nonlocality of the interaction. By considering electron gas layers with varying widths and separations, we derive an analytical expression for the frequency shift relative to the bulk plasmon frequency, valid in the limit of vanishing gap widths. According to our model, if we ignore the electron spill-out, the gap plasmon frequency does not depend on the gap width. However, the electron spill-out and nonlocality of the interaction do affect the gap plasmon behavior, resulting in a logarithmic dependence on the gap width. Notably, if we consider gaps on one side of the interface, the electron spill-out and nonlocality of the interaction do not cancel each other out, resulting in a decrease in the gap plasmon frequency. Our model's findings are in line with a recent study that observed a dip in the gap plasmon frequency, and we attribute this phenomenon to the electron spill-out and nonlocality of the interaction.

In Contextual Named Entity Retrieval, models need to find and link specific entities in unstructured text to a vast knowledge base. Current approaches often ignore the actual context of the entities, which leads to poor performance. To address this issue, a novel response mechanism, referred to as Relevance Response, is proposed to assess the relevance of short phrases in the context, using word representations and contextual information to accurately predict their relevance. This approach is then integrated into Contextual NER to determine the best supporting context for entity disambiguation. Experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate that this response mechanism significantly surpasses the baseline in both entity recall and f1-score metrics.

For analysts to effectively examine time series data, comparing multiple measures across various points in time is essential. This is particularly true in education, healthcare, and other long-term studies. Current data visualization tools can struggle to handle large amounts of data, often failing to engage users or leave users unsure of their interpretation. We provide practical guidance on leading data analysis sessions and report improvements from our office hours sessions. We show that small changes, like using points instead of lines, can make a significant difference in making time series data easier to understand. This is especially true when using interactive visualizations that allow different data measures to be compared side by side. Despite these advancements, most available software still does not effectively handle analysis of multiple measures across various measures. We highlight features from DataSpectra, a tool that facilitates examination of multiple measures, showing how this tool can be used for health and education studies. This is particularly true for longitudinal data, where changes over time can be more easily understood. We show that while DataSpectra is a powerful tool, analysis of multiple measures is particularly challenging when data is missing or if there are gaps in the data.

In recent years, hospital administrators have struggled with managing growing medical data volumes, making task execution increasingly difficult. Extracting useful information from this data while maintaining patient confidentiality poses significant challenges due to privacy concerns and data heterogeneity. Research in medical AI has gained significant momentum, with deep learning at its core, but clinical settings complicate the direct application of machine learning methods due to the diversity of stored medical data. Graph neural networks offer an effective solution for managing unstructured data, making them suitable for electronic health record analysis. We developed a novel GNN model that addresses the inherent heterogeneity of EHRs by representing nodes as distributions of input features. Our method represents EHR nodes as a combination of node type-specific features and shared patient attributes. The model's edge weights represent similarity between nodes and are unique to each patient. This approach allows the GNN to model patient-specific relationships while ignoring irrelevant information. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in EHR node representation, particularly for heterogeneous node prediction tasks. For better interpretability, we employed visualization and feature importance analysis to evaluate the trained model. Our evaluation showed a notable improvement in the performance of our proposed method over existing benchmarks, with more details and source code available at a public repository.

Within the framework of the soft surface model, where the boundary between the skin and core is gradually transitioned, a comprehensive analysis is conducted on the electric double layer formation, taking into account the dynamic interaction between the non-uniform surface charge distribution and the solvent's response. An analytical approach is developed to describe the electric double layer structure, using a general non-ideal model that considers the impact of ion size and solvent permittability variations. The results of this approach are further refined by incorporating the effects of solvent polarization through a first-order perturbation theory. The combination of solvent polarization and non-uniform surface charge distribution significantly affects the electric double layer structure, particularly at low ionic strength conditions, resulting in a more densely packed inner layer and a more gradual outer layer shape compared to standard models. The observed modifications facilitate a greater amount of free ionic charge, thereby enhancing the electrochemical capacity of the interface. These findings are expected to be highly relevant for a wide range of systems characterized by non-uniform surface charge distributions and dynamic solvent interactions.

Extracting relevant information from unstructured text into usable software components can significantly aid the maintenance and development of existing software. This process can be viewed as a machine translation task. Two key aspects must be considered: identifying the importance of individual sentences or parts of sentences and determining the optimal order of relevant information. Existing methods, such as sequence2seq, transformer, and BERT, aim to resolve this issue. However, they face a common challenge of learning from the given data. This paper introduces a novel approach to mitigate these challenges by employing pre-trained models and filtering techniques to refine the extraction process. The proposed method utilizes pre-trained models, filtering by relevance and syntactic analysis to produce acceptable results. The study evaluates this approach using two datasets and compares the outcomes with existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-node wireless network by combining scheduling, power allocation, and network coding techniques. The study specificially analyzes a 6x6 square area with multiple nodes and a single relay node to minimize the total energy consumption in the network. The schedule and power levels are jointly determined through optimization to ensure that the relay node well serves all destinations with a specific rate. The study introduces an energy-efficient network coding scheme that cooperates with the schedule and power allocation designs. The outcomes show that with our proposed method, the energy efficiency in the network is significantly enhanced compared to traditional approaches.

The electronic properties of magnetic adatoms and clusters embedded in a non-magnetic metal can be described by the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states, which are based on relativistic band theory. Previous research used the Anderson impurity model, which doesn't account for the broader band spectrum, whereas our work utilizes the Hartree-Fock Slab-Dirac method to describe the YSR states in detail. This new approach was applied to an Mn adatom and clusters consisting of two and three Mn atoms on the Nb(110) surface and placed in three different magnetic configurations. Results indicate that an Mn adatom and clusters in specific magnetic configurations can display quantized spin torques similar to those found in molecular quantum bits. Moreover, this research demonstrates that an Mn dimer possesses a stable ground state with a remarkably stable spin gap of approximately 350 millielectronvolts, which is remarkably stable and could be applied in stable spin memory.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has announced the initial findings from a search for the rare decay of a kaon into a muon, a pi plus antineutrino. This involved examining 7.2 x 10^12 kaon decays and a 2018 dataset. Only one instance of the desired decay was recorded, as opposed to 0.5 expected occurrences due to background noise and chance probability, thus yielding a confidence level of 0.025+or-0.020 for this occurrence happening by chance. This research resulted in a limit of 10^-10 for this type of decay process, a 2-fold improvement over past studies.

Existing research has effectively applied deep neural network-based algorithms in robotics, particularly in sensor data registration, such as point cloud matching. Nevertheless, these algorithms often perpetuate biases in real-world applications which can lead to inaccurate results. This study aims to address this issue by proposing a framework that combines multiple algorithms and suppresses biased data from the learning process. We developed a filter mechanism which selects reliable data points based on intrinsic characteristics, effectively reducing the impact of biased data. Experimental results using diverse datasets showcase the proposed framework's capability to rectify biases in various distribution-to-distribution matching tasks.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple industries such as agriculture, medicine, and urban planning, with diverse uses ranging from tracking individual trees to managing city traffic. Due to satellite images' relatively low resolution, compared to what is achievable with our daily lives, algorithms struggle to extract useful information from them. With vast areas covered by a single image, algorithms have to be able to process objects that are barely larger than a pixel or up to a hundred hectares in size. With our current knowledge, deep learning has provided the most effective solutions to processing satellite images. Despite being successful, deep learning algorithms exhibit limitations that hinder their usability in everyday applications, such as explaining their actions and adapting to diverse situations. With our current knowledge, a general-purpose tool that can effectively extract edge information from satellite images does not currently exist, with most solutions tailored to specific applications or image types. To address this, we have developed a novel approach to edge detection in satellite images, with our approach outperforming state-of-the-art solutions in multiple benchmarks across various benchmarks and evaluation metrics. With our current implementation, we have achieved high-quality edge detection across diverse scales, with our approach based on novel, cutting-edge methods that enhance edge information extraction. With our knowledge, a user can achieve high-quality edge extraction, with adjustable settings that accommodate various image types and users' needs. With our current knowledge, a user can achieve various applications, with adjustable settings that accommodate various applications and users' needs.

We present a detailed model explaining the resonance peak in high-fluence XANES spectra, focusing on the example of the 1s $\rightarrow$ $\pi^{*}$ transition in copper. The proposed model features a complex resonance shape resulting from interplay between copper's 1s core holes and valence band electron-hole pairs generated by the photon-driven copper band hole. Calculations reveal that each spectral feature arises from core hole interaction with a specific electron density characterized by its momentum. This density is found to be at a maximum around $k_f$ (Fermi wave number) and decrease as momentum deviates from $k_f$. By incorporating this electron density into our model, we have developed a universal rate model describing electron group behavior across many-metal systems and applicable to a wide range of heavy metals and heavy-element compounds spanning across the period table. This model views the 1s core hole as surrounded by a localized electron cloud consisting of two spin-polarized electron spins (one $\uparrow$, one $\downarrow$) and one hole spin ($\uparrow$). In conjunction with the many-body impurity model, we have derived a set of rules governing the distribution of these three spin components. These rules unambiguously determine the spin configuration of the localized electron cloud in the vicinity of the 1s core hole, thus defining the electron group and establishing its spin configuration, which remains unchanged until energy absorption reaches $\sim$1 keV.
