The application of Deep Neural Networks in modulation classification has experienced significant advancements in both research and practical applications. Nevertheless, it is susceptible to attacks beyond the physical realm. Adversarial examples can be generated through a variety of methods, aiming to deceive a DNN and lower its performance. This research presents an innovative approach called the Blend Generative Adversarial Network (B-GAN) to develop a robust modulation classification system that can withstand such attacks. The proposed method integrates the features of multiple DNN models, thereby enhancing the robustness of the system. Experimental results demonstrate that the B-GAN based DNN can successfully classify adversarial examples and maintain high accuracy. Furthermore, its robustness against adversarial attacks surpasses a DNN trained under the Wasserstein constraint.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that repeatedly needs to be addressed across hospitals due to varying data quality and sources. We investigated two techniques, adapting a pre-trained model and learning from scratch, in segmenting lesions in a new hospital's data-set. Given that segmenting individual lesions graphically from MRI images is a common and widely used diagnostic technique, we employed a graph-based deep learning method called GRAKN. We found that pre-training on a large public dataset before fine-tuning it for each individual hospital led to accurate segmention of lesions. This approach outperformed training from scratch on a hospital's specific data-set. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that accurate segmention of lesions can be achieved using deep learning techniques, a crucial step in diagnosing and tracking MS disease activity and response to treatment.

Bipolar contrast refers to the distinction of mental states, sensations, or perceptions using two extreme endpoints or opposites, resulting in the lack of representation for intermediate values and transitions between them. This concept is characterized by the absence of gradual, relative, or fuzzy distinctions, as well as the presence of distinct boundaries and categories. Bipolar contrast is evident in various everyday conversations, readings, and media, and it serves to capture the attention of listeners or readers. This phenomenon is widespread across different cultures and types of texts, including folklore, literature, journalism, social media, and science communication. Bipolar contrast can be attributed to the inherent properties of certain topics or domains and is often employed as a rhetorical device to convey emphasis, but it can also be reduced or mitigated through different presentation methods. Bipolar contrast is an important consideration for authors, policymakers, and scientists due to its potential to influence public perception and action, and it raises significant challenges for communication about complex issues with multiple facets and perspectives.

Our approach for learning model errors in complex systems is adaptable and
component-based, which allows for efficient resolution of statistical issues.
This results in a practical framework that can handle realistic scenarios with
limited computational resources, in contrast to previously proposed formulations.
We employ Bayesian estimation frameworks for model inaccuracies, train the
resulting posterior distributions using supervised learning techniques, and
utilize these trained models for monitoring network performance over time.
This implies that our method achieves optimal statistical results, in the form of
the ideal Bayesian posterior distribution, when the data used to train the model
is sufficiently extensive. We test the effectiveness of our method by applying
it to a hypothetical network with a known solution and model imperfections, and
also discuss how it can be expanded to accommodate more intricate systems with
additional data.

The influence of a parent star on its protostellar cloud is a critical area of study. A notable example of such a relationship occurs in the 'Dragon' infrared cloud, where a large, dark filament is observed to be twisted into intricate structures by the gravitational force of a nearby massive star. Observations of this cloud reveal that the tip of the filament near the star has expanded internally, while its opposite end remains dense and features no signs of a central star. In contrast to typical star-forming clouds, which are usually compressed by external forces, this phenomenon indicates the 'Dragon' cloud has undergone a unique expansion due to the external pressure of the star, while its internal density has decreased. This process is thought to be an early stage in the formation of very massive stars. A proposed model explains the formation of 'S'-shaped structures in the cloud as a result of the star's influence, and supports the initial assumption that the end of the cloud is destined to become a high-mass star.

A novel computational approach named PopSyCLE has been introduced to estimate the potential of dark matter being constituted by primordial black holes. Based on a Bayesian inference framework, PopSyCLE takes into account multiple types of observational data and calculates the constraints they place on the relationship between a black hole's mass (MBH) and its abundance in space. Researchers utilized PopSyCLE to re-examine the possibility of dark matter being composed of primordial black holes under various cosmological theories. The application was particularly interested in investigating the effects of a cosmological model that measures the changes in gravity (MOND) in the universe. The findings revealed that, under a specific model that alters gravity, there are no data constraints that can rule out the possibility of all dark matter existing in the form of primordial black holes with varying initial mass ranges. Conversely, when taking into account a limited effect of these black holes on the cosmic spread of galaxies, no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that primordial black holes alone comprise all of the universe's dark matter, as inferred from various cosmological models. The study's results were consistent with a standard model of the universe for most of its history. The researchers used PopSyCLE to compute the expected characteristics of a primordial black hole's mass distribution should it constitute all of the universe's dark matter. The constraints on a cosmological model that alters gravity were also examined. The findings revealed that current data support a model that alters gravity with a mass range spanning

The phase diagram for a system consisting of wedges formed by three spherical particles has been identified using Monte Carlo simulations. This system exhibits phase stability when it satisfies a geometric constraint, known as the triangular rule. This rule must be adhered to in order for the system to form equilateral triangles on average. If this condition is not met, the system undergoes phase transitions that can be characterized by two distinct order parameters. These order parameters describe triangular structures that arise both with (modulated phase) and without (monolayer phase) breaking the triangular rule. This results in modulated splay and tilt in the modulated phase while the monolayer phase exhibits constant tilt. However, the modulated phase exhibits greater structural stability compared to the monolayer phase due to a stronger attraction between opposing wedges that helps to counteract the effects of splay. This structural preference is more pronounced when the width of the wedges meets a specific criterion. This criterion must be met in order for the system to form larger structures that can result in reduced entropy. If this is not the case, the system exhibits self-assembly into larger structures that can result in reduced entropy. However, when the width of the wedges meets a specific criterion, the system exhibits an entropic preference for smaller units of assembly.

To process special tokens efficiently, most current models employ learned embeddings for these tokens. However, given their predictable nature and limited number, a better approach would be fine-tuning their embeddings alongside the rest of the network. This simple yet effective method proves to be highly efficient and improves the performance of base models, especially in cases where the pre-trained base model was less accurate. Furthermore, there are potential applications for this technique in other areas, such as tokenization and attention distribution. We found through our analysis that the most significant improvements in processing special tokens come from adjusting just one parameter group, and as a result, the remaining adjustments have a relatively minor impact. This led us to develop a technique where the initialization of the adjustments is performed using one-parameter projections from the special token embeddings' gradient expectations.

This paper investigates a distinct preference ordering task that is diverse and covers various types of hierarchical information. The work builds on a context-free preference ordering method introduced by Ultes et al. (2020) and assesses its performance in both non-contextual settings and real-world applications where context is involved. The task under examination is the set addition problem, which entails predicting the cumulative effect of multiple items given their individual properties and potential interactions. To evaluate the performance of the method, a comprehensive dataset was collected and used to develop a baseline comparison with two other recently proposed preference ordering techniques. The results indicate that our approach surpasses the alternatives in both non-contextual and contextual settings. Moreover, fine-tuning the method for the specific task yields a more substantial performance boost, highlighting its potential as a versatile preference ordering method.

Our investigation focuses on the relationship between thermodynamic properties and dynamic characteristics in supercooled and glass-forming polymer liquids.  Utilizing this relationship, we can determine the dynamic properties of these liquids in terms of their thermodynamic states by applying principles of thermodynamics and the idea that dynamics is non-equivalent to equilibrium.  This notion led to the introduction of the concept of "thermodynamic-normalized time", which we utilize in conjunction with the idea that dynamics is non-equivalent to equilibrium.  Applying this to the study of two polymer liquids, we calculated their configurational entropy and tested the relationship between their thermodynamic properties and dynamic characteristics over a wide range of cooling rates.  Our findings demonstrated that accounting for changes in configurational entropy is crucial for capturing the overall shift in the dynamics-principle of dynamic relationships.

Researchers believe that the errors made by language models can provide valuable insights into the models' internal psychology. By examining the mistakes made by models like BERT and GPT-2 in sentence rejection tasks, we investigate the development of rejection reasoning abilities in transformer models. Our study discovers consistent error patterns in rejection tasks, where models incorrectly identify common prepositions as verb modifiers. With this new understanding, we developed RMT, a novel English rejection task that tests the ability to identify verb the prepositions 'about', 'around', and 'across' to correctly recognize verb modifiers. RMT demonstrates excellent performance in different task settings, offering a versatile tool for evaluating the development of rejection reasoning abilities in language models and further understanding their language composition process.

In neural machine translation, the order of words within a sentence influences the accuracy of word translation. To address this challenge, the proposed Look-ahead Focus method focuses on translating words with complex meanings by leveraging context from subsequent sentences. To achieve this, the model considers two encoding methods: one that combines the original sentence context and another that blends the original and following sentences. Experimental results indicate that this approach leads to superior translation quality, particularly for ambiguous words, by optimizing the order of translation. Furthermore, the method allows for the use of flexible window sizes to balance sentence context and translation accuracy. Notably, the model's performance can be harmed if the window size is set too large. Ultimately, the success of this method is supported by analyses from multiple datasets and ambiguous words.

This text provides an overview of the calculation of Kontsevich weights associated with connection and curvature diagrams within the context of symplectic Poisson structures. Building upon initial findings by Merkulov that defined the weights for linear symplectic structures, the study establishes a method for calculating the weights for general symplectic structures. It then demonstrates that the derived formulas can be applied to various special cases, including structures defined by differential forms with specific properties, homogeneous multiplicative structures, and structures tied to L∞-algebras. Furthermore, the research reveals connections between the symplectic connections and curvature diagrams and other fundamental concepts in mathematics and physics, such as Gerstenhaber-Alain Connes-Khovanov weights in cohomology theory and link invariants. The study also delves into the connections between the derived symplectic connections and curvature diagrams and field theories in physics.

This research involves three large-N theories that are variants of a 3D CFT, where the interaction strength varies from non-existent to maximum, with the latter theoretically causing a phase shift. By analyzing the information-to-entropy ratio in both thermal excitations and entanglement among distinct spatial regions within these theories, two types of phase patterns are identified. The patterns in thermal excitations align with previously documented phases, but those for entanglement exhibit an alternative sequence. The reasons behind these differences are explored through the lens of RG trajectories, where thermal excitations mirror thermal entropy behavior and entanglement patterns reflect position-dependent entropy within entanglement wedges. Additionally, this research finds that thermal phases are characterized by conformal dynamics across all couplings, but entanglement phases exhibit a more complex relationship with $N$.

This study builds upon a previous framework developed by Chen et al., which utilizes discrete-time paths to approximate continuous-time Markov chains and calculates the expected value of a payoff function. The framework has been applied to approximate various Asian option pricing methods previously established in the literature. The present research aims to reexamine the efficacy of this framework's implementation of the discrete-time approximation of Markov chains, particularly with regard to the computation of the expected value of a payoff function. Key findings indicate that the direct method of computing the expected value at each time step may not always converge, especially when using a finite state space for the Markov chain. The paper shows that this issue arises due to the payoffs themselves rather than the discrete-time approximation. To address this problem, two alternative methods of expected value calculation are proposed, based on the state distribution and drawn paths. The study also examines the time complexity of these methods and demonstrates their potential for significant performance issues even with relatively small sets of drawn paths due to the growing number of time steps and states. The paper ultimately outlines a set of necessary conditions for a payoff function that ensures the proposed methods will always converge.

We have carried out a study to pinpoint the source of gamma rays from nearby galaxy clusters NOVAE 4, 2003 and RX J0231.1-4420. We have found that the gamma rays in galaxy clusters can be dispersed, meaning they do not necessarily need to originate from the same source as the thermal X-ray radiation. This dispersal criterion has expanded the potential sources of gamma rays to include radio minihalos, supernova shells, and cosmological backgrounds, thereby reducing the need for dark matter annihilation or decay as the primary explanation for the observed gamma ray intensity. Furthermore, our findings suggest that radio minihalos, specifically those with low power, could be the major contributor to the gamma ray emission in galaxy clusters, with the need for additional non-thermal components such as radio relativistic jets or dark matter annialation being less essential.

Our theory, known as classical cosmological collider physics, states that massive particles collide in the early universe, generating specific oscillations or patterns that can be observed in the early universe's primordial properties. These patterns are typically characterized by regular peaks at distinct frequencies. Recently, a model with a single intermediate-mass particle was proposed, which would produce a key frequency in the power spectrum of primordial gravitational waves beyond the primary peak. This model, however, would also predict the appearance of even more pronounced sub-peak frequencies in the spectrum of primordial fluctuations. Our research indicates that the phenomenon can be observed in the gravitational waves spectrum produced by the cosmos' early stages, rather than just primordial fields. These predictions can be tested using various observational data, such as measurements from the Cosmic Microwave Background, primordial fields, and gravitational waves. These findings suggest that the early universe's features can provide a direct link between the cosmos' primordial stages and its current features.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing methods to explain these models can be challenging. Existing techniques, like feature importance, struggle with large-scale image classification tasks. A new method we present uses a filter focus approach, where we represent class meanings with images that can be combined with the model's features to explain its predictions. This approach allows us to identify the specific features relevant to each class and creates a more focused model that makes more interpretable predictions. The effectiveness of our method has been demonstrated on several well-known image classification datasets, and the implementation code is available for free.

The superconducting Cuprates, with their complex properties and enigmatic physics, have garnered substantial research interest. A key aspect of their behavior is the unusual relationship between their electronic properties and structural changes. In this context, a previously unexplored mechanism that contributes to attractive interactions at long ranges is examined. Utilizing theoretical models, simulations, and experiments of related systems, it has been confirmed that attractive interactions are mediated by lattice vibrations. This discovery explains a long-standing observation of a weak binding energy threshold at low temperatures. It has also been found that this phenomenon is linked to a particular vibration frequency variation when the system undergoes structural changes. Additionally, research suggests that this mechanism could enhance the strength of superconducting bonds within self-doped mott insulators.

To protect the health of patients, it is crucial to identify the underlying causes of their adverse reactions to medications. Current algorithms used for causal structural discovery are generally validated using datasets from synthetic origins or studies on individual patients, making them unsuitable for applications involving larger datasets. A recent benchmark dataset from the PHResistant Hypertension dataset is used in this research to test the capabilities of state-of-the-art causal structural discovery algorithms. Due to the presence of time-dependent variables in this dataset, it is necessary to employ advanced methods for handling such variables, making this study unique. Two commonly used algorithms for causal structural discovery are examined in this research, along with the results of various experiments conducted employing different methods for handling time-dependent variables. Our findings indicate that these algorithms can efficiently discover some underlying structures in datasets of smaller sizes, but struggle with the same task in datasets of larger sizes. This study also highlights the need for further validation of causal structural discovery algorithms using datasets of varying sizes.

The discovery of a specific chiral magnet within the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ compound has led to the observation of a stable skyrmion lattice formation, along with the ability to reach the absolute stability point. The absolute stability point is achieved by balancing the balance between the magnetological energy and the magnetization energy through careful adjustment of the temperature. Once reached, this point allows the system to support various topological excitations such as merons and antimerons. Notably, the skyrmion lattice remains stable in the presence of these new topological excitations, demonstrating weak weakening of the skyrmion lattice's stability. The formation of these new excitations occurs through a first-order phase transition and results in a higher skyrmion density, however the energy per skyrmion remains unchanged. The theoretical model suggests that the skyrmion lattice formation occurs due to the skyrmion's energy gain from the surrounding lattice, suggesting that the skyrmion can remain stable in this state. The ability of this system to support various topological excitations makes it an ideal candidate for applications in quantum information storage due to its ability to carry multiple topological charges without destabilizing the skyrmion lattice.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Models, specifically those in time series, pose distinct challenges to statisticians. In such situations, combining data from multiple time points across various variables leads to multifaceted noise patterns, making reliable forecasting and trend identification difficult. Over the years, significant advancements have been made in developing high-dimensional dynamic models, including dynamic factor models, state space models, and various forms of AR and GARCH. In his keynote address, Professor Francq will overview recent breakthroughs in high-dimensional statistics related to time series and highlight potential areas of investigation for the future.

This paper investigates the application of the Picard iteration method in the context of the maximal monotone inclusion problem under the assumption of a nonempty fixed point set for the involved operator. It is demonstrated that this fixed-point approach can provide solutions to the problem without requiring the initial existence of solutions. The results are expandable to address the problem of finding solutions that satisfy multiple inclusion problems. Specifically, for an operator known to have a maximal monotone nature, the paper establishes the condition under which the fixed-point iteration method yields solutions to the problem with minimal error within a specified number of iterations. The findings are illustrated through a practical example.

We develop an innovative technique for hiding visual objects in natural images using reversible concealment. A key constraint of reversible concealment is that the encoded image and decoded representation retain the original texture and retain the same probability distribution as before. Presently, no fully reversible concealment approach is available for complex scenes with non-uniform textures. A recent method overcame this challenge by applying a generative adversarial network (GAN) model to merge the encoded objects into a carrier image, but this approach disregards the probability distribution of the encoded result. In contrast, our proposed framework employs a Bayesian Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) to generate the encoded result. The framework utilizes the posterior distribution of the BNN's learnable parameters to calculate the probability distribution of the encoded result. This novel framework offers the significant advantage of being able to estimate the uncertainty associated with encoded results, which is essential for developing effective methods to detect the presence of forensic traces in encrypted images. Our proposed framework is extensively validated on two benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior concealment quality and reduced artifact rate compared to the existing gan-based approach. Additionally, BNN-based concealment is shown to outperform gan-based concealment in terms of both peak signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity index measure.

The use of mean-field theory in modeling convective dynamos is found to be limited by its assumption that only a select range of wavenumbers needs consideration. In contrast, the development of dynamos often involves higher wavenumbers. In the study of solar convection dynamos, this difference becomes particularly apparent due to the necessity of incorporating smaller-scale turbulent effects to produce stable dynamos. An investigation of convection dynamos in various setups, including ones resembling the Earth's and solar interiors, reveals a common need for including higher wavenumber effects to facilitate stable dynamo operation. In the case of global dynamos, this necessitates taking into account the broader spectrum of turbulent effects available within the mean-field theory, thereby allowing for more comprehensive modeling and understanding of global dynamos.

Our research obtained high-resolution ALMA images of the molecular gas expelled by the central outburst in the NGC 4945 nuclear region using a 12CO(1-0) map with a beam of 0.6", which revealed six distinct molecular gas clumps. Analysis of the gas distribution, velocities, and line widths at 0.6" and 0.8" resolution showed self-consistency and self-absorption. The gas clumps have velocities ranging from -260 to -120 km/s. The line widths of the gas clumps are broadly estimated at 40-70 km/s. The gas clumps can be divided into two groups based on their positions, with the more eastern group showing lower velocities. Observations of the continuum and CO absorption lines provide evidence for gas clumps at the nuclear region of NGC 4945.

A magnetized plasma's thermal equilibrium is effectively described by the quasilinear diffusion framework. This model reduces kinetic plasma simulations' computational requirements while retaining essential magnetic and energetic properties. This study presents a new solver for the quasilinear diffusion framework that is implemented in magnetostatic regime. A fully implicit time-stepping scheme is developed in conjunction with high-order Galerkin discretization methods for the spatial domains. Due to the inclusion of collisional terms, the proposed solver is thoroughly analyzed to guarantee the conservation of key physical properties. Furthermore, the solver is implemented in a unified framework with arbitrary spatial and temporal discretization methods. As a demonstration of its capabilities, the new solver is applied to multiple plasma physics scenarios and its results are compared to established reference values.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods with non-uniform stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs), and prove that a specific variable stepsize implementation satisfies the required order conditions without additional constraints on its construction. We also demonstrate and test a variable stepsize implementation for solving first-order differential equations efficiently.

This paper investigates the relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T(t) and solutions (A(t), P(t))-(A, P) to the Lyapunov equation. Specifically, we establish that if there exists a bounded and invertible sequence of operators P(t) such that the associated Lyapunov equation has a solution, and a bound can be placed on the maximal subvariety of t ∈ [0, ∞) for which the residual map has a closed range, then stability is equivalent to the existence and uniqueness of the solution (A(t), P(t)) under certain conditions on the derivative d_A(t)P(t)/dt and the strong left topological regularity of T(t). Additionally, we present an example demonstrating the significance of the conditions on the maximal subvariety.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software for determining how dimuonium binds with substances in its ground state, which is based on the potential distribution model and the Kohn-Sham density functional theory, enabling the prediction of dimuonium's spectral lines and chemical reactivity. The code also includes features for calculating the binding energy, charge distribution, and spectral line intensity of dimuonium with respect to different substances, which can be visualized through 3D plots. MuMuPy utilizes the NumPy and PyFMpy libraries, offering a user-friendly interface through the execution of Python commands. It includes examples of dimuonium binding with hydrogen, water, and dimethylsulfuric acid, as well as a table comparing the predicted binding energies to theoretical and experimental values, especially for dimuonium's interaction with sulfuric acid. MuMuPy is available in open-source form at https://github.com/mumupy/MuMuPy.

This study enhances portfoliomanagement by applying a power utility function, taking into account both absolute and relative wealth variations. The latter is intended to reduce variability in relative outcomes. The direct calculation method previously used for absolute wealth is found to be impractical for absolute-relative wealth combinations due to computational and spatial issues. An MCMC algorithm is thus employed to generate optimal outcomes. A numerical analysis demonstrates that a combination of both absolute and relative wealths can yield lower volatility and greater expected utility in comparison to absolute wealth alone. Ultimately, a higher utility is achieved through an optimal asset allocation that balances stability and growth.

The morphology of galaxies is closely linked to their stellar mass and environmental factors. Small, low-metallic galaxies known as dwarf galaxies reside predominantly in secluded areas of space and are influenced by a limited number of external factors. Researchers have recently made significant progress in studying the intergalactic matter within dwarf galaxies through advanced spectrographic analysis. This investigation focuses on presenting new measurements of IGM within dwarf galaxies, examining the link between IGM properties, a galaxy's mass, and its location within a given mass bin. Additionally, the study compares IGM characteristics within early-type and late-type dwarf galaxies. Our findings reveal IGM properties within dwarf galaxies to be similar to those found in larger spiral galaxies, suggesting a mass-dependent correlation. Furthermore, the study reveals striking contrasts between Igalactic and IGM temperatures within close groups of galaxies, while observing no significant temperature variations within the aformentioned groups. Our analysis also detects a lack of gas within very low-mass galaxies, which may be a characteristic unique to these systems.

We examine the distinct characteristics of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermionic polaron model, where the unitary limit has significant implications for the formation of these quasiparticles. In this model, the combined effect of a fermion and a local boson results in an average total spin of 1/2, with the quasiparticle character emerging when this spin is largely condensed. Notably, our investigation highlights the unusual behavior of the quasiparticle in the presence of a strong attractive potential, where the Ubershock regime deviates from the Shockley regime due to the activation of Ubershock eigenstates, leading to increased energies within these states. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the quasiparticle characteristic is highly sensitive to the occupation of the bosonic state, with the loss of this occupation resulting in an abrupt shift from the Ubershock to Shockley regimes. In contrast, the occupation of multiple bosonic states in the Ubershock regime leads to a decrease in these states, while the quasiparticle character persists, with the system exhibiting a superfluid state in the Ubershock regime that is distinct from the Shockley regime.

G. Thompson's groups form a notable class of infinite but finite presentations groups.
In this context, we explore the divergence properties within three distinct group types:
specifically, the Thompson's groups V, V1, and V1~, each exhibiting distinct properties.
Notably, our findings indicate that V diverges freely and uniformly, whereas V1 and V1~ each exhibit free, uniform, and hyperbolic divergences.
The braided Thompson groups, particularly BR and LBR, are found to diverge freely, uniformly, and hyperbolically as well.
Investigations into the relationships between these groups lead to notable observations regarding their cardinal divergences.

This paper explores the application of the recently introduced Retrieval Augmented Generation model, specifically using the Complete RAG architecture from GitHub, to address question-answering. This model aggregates responses from both a pre-trained transformer and a pre-trained retriever. We've adapted the Complete RAG architecture to source our data from the DocVQA 3.0 dataset, which necessitates three answers. We've also modified the Complete RAG loss function to accommodate multi-answer questions. Initially, the model retrieves relevant documents for each question and extracts answers that match the question's context. We've implemented additional strategies to enhance the model's performance, including filtering retrieved documents based on answer uniqueness and incorporating a correct answer filter. We've also created a dataset sub-sampler to maintain a minimum of three answers per question. We've fine-tuned the Complete RAG model using the accuracy@1 measure. Notably, the model achieved an accuracy of 66.2% when only considering the top answer and 80.6% for all retrieved answers. We've evaluated the model's generalization performance by training it on the training dataset and testing it on an unseen validation set. We've also compared the model's performance to the deep learning baseline and established a significant 50.2% performance gap. We've conducted an ablation study to assess the influence of the correct answer filter and sub-sampling strategy on the model's performance. Notably, the strategy had a substantial impact, with performance degradation

This paper introduces a logarithmic weight function, specifically $\log(1+y)$, and examines the limiting characteristics of the orthogonal polynomials resulting from this function on the interval $(0,1)$ and $(0,\infty)$. Subsequently, we considers a broader family of weights with the same underlying logarithmic behavior, and provides asymptotic analyses for the associated orthogonal polynomials, as well as the associated Markov chains and linear differential equations. These analyses reveal a variety of intriguing asymptotic patterns.

The vast pool of workers on crowdsourcing platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk is seen as an ideal resource for completing small tasks that require specific skills. Researchers and practitioners rely on these platforms to recruit workers with particular qualifications. However, identifying and appointing the right workers remains a significant challenge. We investigated this issue by collecting data on our own crowdsourcing experiment, where we evaluated the effectiveness of using qualifications to identify skilled workers. Our results indicate that workers may overstate their qualifications, and even if they have the required skills, they may lack the necessary knowledge. We also found that some workers with the necessary skills may choose not to participate in our study, and those who do participate may not always provide accurate answers.

Our proposed TS2-Net is a retrieval framework for long-text queries and compressed text clips. It simplifies complex queries by breaking them down into distinct tokens and assigning variable-length significance to each. TS2-Net asks a secondary question beyond traditional similarity measures: given a variable number of tokens from the query and the clip, which tokens from each should be prioritized? TS2-Net's answer lies in its innovative transformer architecture and associated training objectives. Initially, it streamlines queries and clips through reduction, before identifying the most relevant segments by asking a query-like question and engaging in a self-attention process. Finally, it merges the most significant tokens from each source to determine their level of similarity. Extensive testing using the TREC Text-Clip dataset demonstrates TS2-Net's exceptional performance across various retrieval scenarios.

The concept of flavour change for charged particles originates from beyond standard model physics, where taste-changing neutral currents in fermions have a comparable effect. Despite the lack of data on neutral flavour changing processes in fermions, multi-Higgs models predict them, especially in fermions other than top quarks. A new model we present includes a flavour-dependent neutral current in the top sector, with the lightest flavour-changing neutral current in top quarks potentially detectable at the Large Hadron Collider with reasonable sensitivity, especially with the reach of the HL-LHC in the decay chain $t\rightarrow h c$, and at proposed facilities like the Future Circular Collider, especially with the reach of the FCC-hh in the decay chain $t\rightarrow h g$.

In the realm of complex network analysis, researchers often explore various growth and link formation processes beyond simple random graphs. This investigation focuses on a specific model, hybrid random graph, which combines a preferential attachment mechanism with uniform attachment, distinguishing old vertices from new ones based on their ages. This model deviates from standard models in the literature by incorporating both preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. This work delves into understanding the structural characteristics of the resulting graphs, which exhibit characteristics of scale-free networks, self-similarity, and small-world properties. A comprehensive statistical analysis is provided, along with an examination of outliers in in-degree and strong in-degree distributions, through the use of Q-Q plots and return probability distributions. A comparison with other well-known models, including Erdos-Renyi random graphs, preferential attachment, uniform attachment, and directed scale-free networks, highlights the distinct properties of in-degree, strong in-degree, and out-degree distributions in the proposed hybrid graph model.

The proliferation of wireless communication systems has raised concerns about interference due to increasing use of the wireless spectrum. Distinguishing the source and type of interference is crucial for system operators to mitigate it. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying multiple types of wireless disturbances encountered by television receivers. The proposed method utilizes convolutional neural networks to classify disturbance images or audio waveforms, with the option to expand this approach to identify multiple disturbance types. Experimental results demonstrate that the suggested technique is more accurate than a comparative established method.

To grasp the impact of spacetime defects, we examine the movement of both charged and uncharged Klein-Gordon particles in a cosmic string spacetime with flaws, considering various types of flaws characterized by different gravitational potential surfaces. To this end, we focus on a specific type of flaw described by the function $G(\xi)$ and derive exact solutions of the relevant Klein-Gordon equations for both particles, calculating their full probability distributions in the process. Our findings indicate that the probabilities of finding the particles within the event horizon or outside the event horizon are influenced by the parameter $p$, with the probabilities being maximized when the particles are at or outside the event horizon. Additionally, we analyze the correlations between the creation and loss of particles in relation to the particle's vortex state and its position relative to the event horizon. Our analysis shows that the sign of these correlations can be modified by the parameter $\eta$ if the particles are located inside the event horizon, whereas no such influence is observed if the particles are at or outside the event horizon.
Countable, finitely generated measure algebras that incorporate locally usual elements are classified.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood by analyzing specific interactions between a proton and a photon, specifically at a very high energy and with a very small distance. Researchers focus on one such interaction, known as deep-virtual photon scattering (DVCS), and are trying to find a way to measure its effects accurately. An innovative approach has been suggested that relies on the polarization of a proton that "recoils" after being hit by a photon in a particular direction. By studying this phenomenon, known as $${\cal{P}}_n$$, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how partons within a proton are connected. An in-depth analysis is provided on measuring $${\cal{P}}_n$$ using a high-energy collider that produces real or virtual photons, and its detectability is discussed using CLAS12 experiment data. By comparing different methods to measure DVCS effects, known as parton distribution functions (PDFs), the distinct role of $${{\cal{P}}_n}}$$ in constraining a key photon-proton interaction tensor, known as $${\cal{T}}_{\Gamma}$$, is explained within the context of a particular photon-proton scattering process that occurs at a very high energy.
